title: The Chiefs might have whiffed on their 2025 free agency class
summary: In sports, much like in life, actions speak louder than words. Few moments offer a clearer window into how an organization views its roster than free agency. Teams spend millions of dollars to fill holes, and those investments reveal exactly how the front office evaluates its personnel. The draft does the same. Training camp provides […]
full_text: In sports, much like in life, actions speak louder than words. Few moments offer a clearer window into how an organization views its roster than free agency. Teams spend millions of dollars to fill holes, and those investments reveal exactly how the front office evaluates its personnel. The draft does the same. Training camp provides another revealing checkpoint. It’s the first real opportunity for fans to see how the coaching staff views its current options. Starting reps are limited. Time with the first team is valuable. So it stands out when surprise Kansas City Chiefs players get run with the first team, especially when that first team includes Patrick Mahomes. I wrote last week about two players , wide receiver Cyrus Allen and offensive tackle Kahlil Benson, whose opportunities with Mahomes caught my attention. At the time, I viewed those reps as more meaningful for their long-term outlook than for the 2026 season. It’s becoming increasingly difficult to ignore Benson’s role on this team. As best I can tell from following camp, Benson has opened virtually every practice as the starting right tackle. At some point, that has to carry weight. Rotating with the starters is one thing. It’s another thing entirely when you’re getting the same treatment with the first-team offense as Josh Simmons, Kingsley Suamataia, Creed Humphrey and Trey Smith. I wish I could say that gives me warm, fuzzy feelings. It doesn’t. Benson is a fun story, but this development seems to say more about Jaylon Moore than it does about Benson. Last year’s $30 million signing suddenly looks like a sixth offensive lineman instead of a starting tackle. That’s not what the Chiefs thought they were buying. If Benson really is winning this job, then Moore’s contract stops being just a roster decision. It becomes an expensive miss for a front office that can’t afford many of them. I’ve said all offseason I’m confused by the buzz about the Chiefs’ interest in tackles. Why would they already look for an off-ramp when they paid so handsomely in the market for the player they hoped would be their 2026 stopgap for the only open position on the roster? But the buzz wouldn’t go away. First it was free agency. Then the draft. National insiders kept linking the Chiefs to tackles. I couldn’t wrap my mind around it. Now, I can. Did the Chiefs know all along they were sold a lemon in Moore? And if they did, why didn’t they make a more aggressive push to protect their franchise quarterback coming off a serious knee injury? The truth is the Chiefs have been hamstrung all offseason by last year’s free agent class. Moore is on the books for $18.6 million this year. Only Chris Jones, Mahomes, Smith and Nick Bolton have larger cap hits for the 2026 campaign. Kristian Fulton ranks seventh on the team with a $13 million cap hit. Moore and Fulton combine for $32 million against the cap. Jauan Jennings, Jadeveon Clowney, Tariq Woolen and Jermaine Eluemunor signed for a combined $31 million this year against the cap. Only Eluemunor of that group is on a multi-year deal. Woof. The Chiefs are still paying for last year’s spending spree. Both figuratively and literally. Their cap hits are rising as their roles are shrinking. Maybe none of this will matter. Maybe Benson instantly develops into an above-average starter, and the cornerback depth minimizes the risk of missing or whiffing on Fulton. That’s the optimists’ outlook, at least. The reality is Kansas City’s cap situation leaves little room for expensive mistakes. Right now, the returns on last year’s free-agent class aren’t trending in the right direction. Actions speak louder than words, and the Chiefs’ actions are revealing their updated view of how Fulton and Moore fit into their 2026 plans.

title: Kurt Warner, not Torry Holt, was the GSOT beneficiary
summary: Whenever the “Greatest Show on Turf” is discussed, the spotlight almost always lands on Kurt Warner. As a two-time NFL MVP, Super Bowl champion, and Pro Football Hall of Famer, Warner’s story is one of the greatest in football history. His journey from stocking grocery store shelves to leading one of the most explosive offenses […]
full_text: Whenever the “Greatest Show on Turf” is discussed, the spotlight almost always lands on Kurt Warner. As a two-time NFL MVP, Super Bowl champion, and Pro Football Hall of Famer, Warner’s story is one of the greatest in football history. His journey from stocking grocery store shelves to leading one of the most explosive offenses ever assembled is legendary. But here’s a question that deserves more discussion: if anyone truly benefited the most from the Rams’ historic supporting cast, wasn’t it Warner rather than Torry Holt? This isn’t an argument against Warner’s Hall of Fame credentials. He earned his place in Canton, and his accomplishments deserve recognition. Instead, it’s an argument that Torry Holt’s Hall of Fame candidacy should not continue to be delayed simply because people remember Warner first when they think about those Rams offenses. https://t.co/ZvHMroh9PW — EssentiallySports (@ES_sportsnews) January 30, 2026 Warner stepped into arguably the most complete offensive situation in the NFL. The Rams featured one of football’s premier offensive lines, anchored by Orlando Pace and Adam Timmerman. They had NFL MVP Marshall Faulk in the backfield, a player who could dominate games as both a runner and receiver. Then there were two elite wide receivers in Isaac Bruce and Torry Holt, giving defenses impossible choices every Sunday. Few quarterbacks in league history have inherited that level of offensive talent. Warner’s 1999 season was unquestionably one of the greatest quarterback seasons ever. He threw for 4,353 yards, 41 touchdowns, won league MVP honors, and led the Rams to a Super Bowl victory. No one should minimize that accomplishment. Kurt Warner finds @AllHands81 Torry Holt for the 45 yard score against the Miami defense – 2001. Way to hang in there @kurt13warner and deliver the strike for pay dirt. pic.twitter.com/KXby70fYaZ — RAMS ON FILM (@RamsOnFilm) November 8, 2024 However, when looking at his Rams tenure as a whole, that 1999 campaign stands apart from the rest. Warner won another MVP award in 2001, but that season wasn’t nearly as clean as many remember. While he threw 36 touchdown passes, he also tossed 22 interceptions, one of the highest totals in the league that year. Across his six seasons with the Rams, spanning just 53 games, Warner threw 102 touchdown passes against 65 interceptions. Those numbers are productive, but they also reflect a quarterback who was willing to take risks and occasionally struggled with turnovers. In contrast, Torry Holt’s excellence wasn’t confined to one magical stretch. Holt produced regardless of who lined up behind center. Whether it was Warner, Marc Bulger, Jamie Martin, Ryan Fitzpatrick, or others forced into action because of injuries, Holt continued to post elite production. Defenses knew he was the focal point of the passing attack, yet he consistently found ways to create separation, make contested catches, and produce explosive plays. That consistency is what should define his legacy. From 2000 through 2005, Holt recorded six consecutive 1,300-yard receiving seasons, an NFL record that still stands. He surpassed 90 receptions seven times and finished his career with 920 catches, 13,382 receiving yards, and 74 touchdowns despite playing during an era loaded with Hall of Fame-caliber receivers. Torry Holt was arguably the best wide receiver in the NFL in the 2000s. Unlike quarterbacks, who naturally receive much of the credit when offenses succeed, wide receivers are dependent on others to get them the football. Holt never had the luxury of playing his entire career with one elite quarterback. Instead, he adjusted to changing offensive coordinators, different quarterbacks, and an evolving Rams roster while remaining one of the league’s most dependable stars. If anything, Warner benefited from Holt’s ability to turn routine throws into chunk gains just as much as Holt benefited from Warner’s arm. The conversation surrounding the Greatest Show on Turf often credits Warner as the engine that made everything work. But it could just as easily be argued that Warner was placed into the perfect environment: an elite offensive line, the league’s most versatile running back in Faulk, and two future Hall of Fame-caliber receivers in Bruce and Holt. Meanwhile, Holt proved something that every Hall of Fame voter should appreciate—he produced regardless of circumstance. That’s ultimately why his Hall of Fame case should stand on its own. Warner has already received the recognition he deserved, and rightly so. Now it’s time for Holt to receive his. His sustained excellence, remarkable consistency, and ability to thrive no matter who was throwing him the football should remove any remaining doubt. The Greatest Show on Turf was filled with stars. But if we’re talking about who truly benefited the most from that extraordinary collection of talent, the answer may not be Torry Holt. It may have been Kurt Warner.
author: Steven Ridings

title: Cardinals might not be the pushover we expect
summary: The Arizona Cardinals, and especially Carson Beck, turned a lot of heads Thursday night. Most everyone expects the Los Angeles Rams’ divisional foe to be one of the NFL’s worst teams, but could the Cardinals actually surprise this season? Before we go too far off the deep end, this was only one preseason game. A […]
full_text: CANTON, OHIO - AUGUST 06: Head coach Mike LaFleur of the Arizona Cardinals looks on during the first quarter of the 2026 Pro Football Hall of Fame Game against the Carolina Panthers at Tom Benson Hall Of Fame Stadium on August 06, 2026 in Canton, Ohio. (Photo by Nick Cammett/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Arizona Cardinals, and especially Carson Beck, turned a lot of heads Thursday night. Most everyone expects the Los Angeles Rams’ divisional foe to be one of the NFL’s worst teams, but could the Cardinals actually surprise this season? Before we go too far off the deep end, this was only one preseason game. A stellar showing in the Hall of Fame Game obviously doesn’t mean Arizona is destined for a playoff run or a finish anywhere close to .500. However, they showed enough flashes in Canton that they might not be a complete pushover in 2026. Fans and analysts have rightfully given Carson Beck his flowers for a strong NFL debut, but what about first-year head coach Mike LaFleur? The former Rams assistant coach, in his first game calling the shots, guided the Cardinals to rolling up 425 yards of offense. Arizona rushed for 143 yards (4.2 yards per attempt) and converted on 7-of-12 third-down attempts. If that’s how the unit performs without its primary starters in the lineup, imagine the damage they’ll do once the regular season kicks off. Still, Beck was sensational and quite poised against Carolina. He finished 15-of-19 for 188 yards and one touchdown, delivering several accurate passes and demonstrating veteran presence in the pocket throughout. Additionally, he also led a 98-yard touchdown drive in the first half. Jacoby Brissett shouldn’t have much to worry about for now, but if he struggles to start the season, the calls for Beck to start will grow louder in the desert. View this post on Instagram Again, this was only one preseason game, which rarely means anything once the real games begin. But the game showed that maybe the Cardinals are finally on the right path. They do have an extremely low bar to clear. As I noted ahead of the NFL draft , Arizona has gone 19-49 from 2022 to 2025 , including three double-digit loss campaigns. They’ve also made five postseason appearances this century, including once in the last decade (2021). The Cardinals’ playoff drought is four seasons and counting, with one winning season since advancing to the 2015 NFC Championship. LaFleur doesn’t need to be a miracle worker in Year 1. Instead, he needs to guide his team towards progress, which shouldn’t be too difficult, given the Redbirds are coming off a three-win campaign. The Cardinals have the worst odds to make the playoffs in the NFC (+2000), according to FanDuel Sportsbook . Despite that, ESPN NFL analyst Louis Riddick said on “The Dan Patrick Show” this week that he believes in Arizona’s potential, thanks to its young roster. Riddick could be onto something. The Cardinals will likely be the worst team in the loaded NFC West this season, but that doesn’t mean they can’t put some scares into the Rams, Seahawks and 49ers along the way. Thursday was certainly a promising start to the LaFleur era in Arizona, and perhaps it could be the start of good things to come for a franchise that sorely needs it.
author: Evan Craig

title: How Horrible is Nick Wright’s Aaron Donald Take?
summary: The worst version of Aaron Donald that we’ve ever seen was still the best interior pass rusher in the NFL, but sports commentator Nick Wright still thinks that was a sign of too much of a decline for the L.A. Rams’ great to return to the team this year. Is Wright’s take on Aaron Donald […]
full_text: Inglewood, CA - February 08: Los Angeles Rams defensive end Aaron Donald (99) is interviewed after defeating the Cincinnati Bengals 23-20 in Super Bowl LVI at SoFi Stadium on Monday, Feb. 8, 2016 in Inglewood, CA. (Wally Skalij / Los Angeles Times via Getty Images) The worst version of Aaron Donald that we’ve ever seen was still the best interior pass rusher in the NFL, but sports commentator Nick Wright still thinks that was a sign of too much of a decline for the L.A. Rams’ great to return to the team this year. Is Wright’s take on Aaron Donald the worst we’ve seen this year? On First Things First, Wright responds to co-host Chris Broussard’s opinion that Donald will return by saying that AD was “not the player that he was and not the player that he wanted to be” in 2022 and 2023. “I don’t think [Donald’s] coming back… I think if he did come back, he’d be good… But I think he already, his last two years, was not the player that he was & the player that he wanted to be… If he comes back, it’s… a zero downside proposition.” Wright calls Donald’s last year one of the worst of his career. Which, to be clear, included a first-team All-Pro selection, eight sacks, and 23 QB hits. Only two defensive tackles had more QB hits that year (Nnamdi Madubuike and Chris Jones). “I don’t think [Donald's] coming back… I think if he did come back, he’d be good… But I think he already, his last two years, was not the player that he was & the player that he wanted to be… If he comes back, it's… a zero downside proposition.” @getnickwright explains: pic.twitter.com/qlD2cvRZur — First Things First (@FTFonFS1) August 6, 2026 Per PFF, Donald’s last two seasons saw him ranked third and second among all defensive tackle grades, following a streak of seven consecutive years at number one. Aaron Donald year by year Defensive Grades Interior DL Rank 2023 90.8 2nd 2022 90.5 3rd 2021 93.5 1st 2020 94.2 1st 2019 93.6 1st 2018 94.8 1st 2017 94.4 1st 2016 92.6 1st… pic.twitter.com/FRyiAy0ONz — PFF (@PFF) August 5, 2026 Wright frames Donald’s two years as if he was as different as Aaron Rodgers has been since tearing his Achilles, when in fact Donald was an elite defensive tackle when he retired. That’s why many were caught off-guard when Donald retired. Now Wright is framing it as if Donald walked away because he was declining. Instead of what it actually was, which was a chance to retire without a decline. Furthermore, Nick Wright practically makes something up during his argument. He says that “I looked at one of (Aaron Donald)’s comments about (returning) only if he’s at the level that he’s accustomed to”. Donald never said that. It’s well known that Aaron Donald has not directly said anything to the media about coming back, with the exception of maybe a few text messages, which are also hearsay. Wright is making it sound as though Aaron Donald released a statement saying, “I will return only if I’m the same as I’m accustomed to.” At best, Wright is taking something that Sean McVay said and attributing it to Donald . Which a journalist should not do. Second of all, what is Aaron Donald “accustomed to” anyway, Nick? Because he retired as one of the top-three defensive tackles in the NFL. What is it about Donald’s last two years that suggests anything different? Maybe we should ask any offensive lineman who blocked Donald in 2023, “Hey was that easy?” and let’s see if anyone says that it was, that it was easy. Probably not. Probably not easier either. What Wright got Right Look more people should be questioning whether or not Donald is even going to be a very good player if he returns. Donald is 35 and he hasn’t played since 2023 and he may have had an easier time getting ready for the season if he had made this decision in February. On that point, I think Wright is choosing the more difficult side to defend and could be commended for not just repeating what everyone else is saying, which is that Donald will “surely” be great if he returns. Maybe he won’t be great at all. However, Wright’s points (which, if we’re being totally fair, were probably scripted based off of the show’s need to have a debate and not necessarily actual thoughts that he has) miss the mark. They’re not good debate points. Donald’s last two seasons should have nothing to do with whether or not he can be great next season because he was still great when he retired. This is not the same as Philip Rivers returning in 2025, when Philip Rivers was already showing major signs of decline when he retired five years earlier. Donald hasn’t show any decline. And by all accounts, Donald was probably even better in 2023 than he was at times during his first three seasons in the NFL. So even if Wright’s right to question if Donald can still dominate as he used to in the NFL, Wright’s wrong to use mediocre talking points and quotes that never happened to try and make that argument.
author: Kenneth Arthur

title: Report: If Aaron Donald returns, it should be soon
summary: If the rumors about Aaron Donald’s desire to come out of retirement to join the Los Angeles Rams for 2026 come true, then the three-time Defensive Player of the Year will probably announce a decision in the near future, according to ProFootballTalk’s Mike Florio. Donald has been dominating the NFL news cycle more than basically […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - NOVEMBER 15: Former Pittsburgh Panthers player Aaron Donald during his jersey retirement ceremony at halftime of the game between the Pittsburgh Panthers and the Notre Dame Fighting Irish at Acrisure Stadium on November 15, 2025 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by G Fiume/Getty Images) | Getty Images If the rumors about Aaron Donald’s desire to come out of retirement to join the Los Angeles Rams for 2026 come true, then the three-time Defensive Player of the Year will probably announce a decision in the near future, according to ProFootballTalk’s Mike Florio. Donald has been dominating the NFL news cycle more than basically any player who is actually active in the league right now, so it’s not surprising that Florio—and all reporters—would like an answer soon. But will that actually be the case? Florio says he is just the messenger, but he claims to have a reliable source who reportedly told Florio that either Donald returns, and it could be announced “very soon”, or Donald doesn’t plan to return, and nothing will be said. Plenty of variables but here’s Florio’s full quote from PFT Live: “If he’s going to do it, and it’s ultimately his decision, he’s going to do it…we could hear something very soon. Today’s the 7th (of August). We could hear something very soon. Don’t be surprised…if he’s not, we’re not gonna hear anything, but if he is…we’re gonna hear something very soon.” Florio goes on to share that former head coach and now talking head Mike Tomlin doesn’t expect Donald to be back soon, but rather that the Rams want him for a playoff push. Tomlin doesn’t claim to have a source, but that’s how he views it. We don’t have certainty on the Donald situation (though by the time you see this we might), but in theory and according to Florio, if Donald is back, we’ll know very soon. If he’s not, we won’t hear a word. Florio says “don’t be surprised” , but Donald coming back would be surprising, so stay tuned. Though it’s not likely anyone will miss the announcement that is made if AD does return. File this one away under: Keep your eyes and ears open, in the Turf Show Times Zone.
author: Danny Stone

title: As Rams put off extending guards, another gets paid
summary: The Los Angeles Rams have two starting guards entering a contract year, but as general manager Les Snead mulls over what Kevin Dotson and Steve Avila are worth, the Buffalo Bills struck a four-year, $78.4 million deal with O’Cyrus Torrence. The Bills extending Torrence to a deal paying him almost $20 million per season may […]
full_text: DENVER, CO - JANUARY 17: Buffalo Bills guard O'Cyrus Torrence (64) walks onto the field to warm up before the AFC Divisional Round game against the Denver Broncos at Empower Field at Mile High on January 17, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Dustin Bradford/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Los Angeles Rams have two starting guards entering a contract year, but as general manager Les Snead mulls over what Kevin Dotson and Steve Avila are worth, the Buffalo Bills struck a four-year, $78.4 million deal with O’Cyrus Torrence. The Bills extending Torrence to a deal paying him almost $20 million per season may not seem like it matters to the Rams, but NFL contracts are like a conga line that you don’t want to be at the back of. As the Rams wait, the price for Dotson and Avila rises. Sources: The #Bills and G O'Cyrus Torrence agreed to terms on a 4-year, $78.4M extension, as the former 2nd rounder cashes in. 7th highest paid guard. He gets more than $46M guaranteed in a deal done by agents Jon Perzley, Brian Mackler, and Daniel Scardigno of @SPORTSTARSNYC . pic.twitter.com/qKXUXnHdoX — Ian Rapoport (@RapSheet) August 7, 2026 Torrence is hardly the best guard in the NFL, and that’s actually worse news for the Rams than if he was. The move means that a three-year starter with no Pro Bowl appearances now costs $20 million per season. Guess who else is a three-year starter with no Pro Bowl appearances. Steve Avila. Torrence was taken 23 picks after L.A. chose Avila out of TCU, and in a rough manner their careers are the same. Buffalo couldn’t wait any longer to make sure that they didn’t have to go out and find a different guard in 2027, so will the Rams do the same soon with Avila? He’s the same age as Torrence and will probably command at least $20 million annually if he reaches free agency in 2027. The problem for L.A. could just be deciding between Avila and Dotson. Kevin Dotson is better, but older Torrence’s deal makes him the seventh-highest paid guard in the NFL overall, but Dotson is the seventh-highest paid right guard in the NFL right now, at $16 million per season. Almost 30, Dotson’s next contract should challenge Trey Smith, at $23.5 million AAV, for the highest in the league at right guard. LAFB Network recently highlighted Dotson’s value as a mentor at training camp : Dotson’s work with Warren McClendon Jr. stood out. Dotson and McClendon were nearly inseparable between periods, with the veteran guard repeatedly coaching up the younger tackle. McClendon followed with encouraging reps against Stewart and a deep edge group. The pair also combined to double-team Kobie Turner, while Steve Avila kept Turner under control on another snap. At this point in camp, that communication matters almost as much as an isolated win because it shows how the offensive line is building continuity behind its established starters. Do the Rams have enough cap space to pay both Dotson and Avila? Well, in theory, sure. Whether or not they want to is a more important question. It’s not clear if the Rams have good, bad, or indifferent depth at guard, but they did draft Keagen Trost in the third round to give themselves options. Between Puka Nacua, Kobie Turner, Byron Young, and others, it won’t be easy to predict which players the Rams will keep, and that could even be true for Snead. However, the longer he waits, the more expensive these players get. Conga.
author: Kenneth Arthur

title: Terrance Ferguson is the unlikely key to Rams’ next step
summary: The Rams player who could be L.A.’s most direct path to hitting their next level on offense is second-year tight end Terrance Ferguson. It’s easy to get overlooked on a team this talented, and Ferguson’s rookie season was one he’d probably like to forget on some level, but he may also hold the key to […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - NOVEMBER 09: Terrance Ferguson #18 of the Los Angeles Rams runs with the ball against the San Francisco 49ers in the first quarter at Levi's Stadium on November 09, 2025 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Rams player who could be L.A.’s most direct path to hitting their next level on offense is second-year tight end Terrance Ferguson. It’s easy to get overlooked on a team this talented, and Ferguson’s rookie season was one he’d probably like to forget on some level, but he may also hold the key to the offense becoming a juggernaut. Most of the Rams’ biggest contributors are mostly known commodities at this point, considering guys like Matthew Stafford, Kyren Williams, Puka Nacua, Davante Adams and most of the offensive line. Colby Parkinson and Tyler Higbee, two other members of the tight ends room, also fall under that description. But Ferguson, at least based on his athletic profile and collegiate tape, still has plenty of room between his current form and his ceiling. Rams can still keep getting better It’s hard to improve on being the best team at anything in the NFL. The talent gap, even between the best and worst teams, is truly quite slim, and the league is constructed in a way that generally pulls the great teams down over time and lifts the bad teams up. The Los Angeles Rams are entering 2026 with a huge target on their backs. No, they aren’t the reigning champions, but they were widely considered the best team in the league last year and they were undoubtedly the best offense. It’s hard to argue with being No. 1 in scoring, total offense, passing offense, success rate … you get the gist. But if you’re not constantly evolving, your stay at or near the top in the NFL isn’t going to be there for very long. Thus, the Rams need to do something this year to stay in front of the pack. Ferguson’s unique skillset Ferguson was a great athletic tester coming out of Oregon, posting an elite 9.57 RAS with a tantalizing combination of raw speed and explosiveness. And he showed off that expected big-play ability last season, only catching 11 passes as a rookie but averaging 21 yards per reception. What’s more, nine of those 11 receptions (and 10 of 12 if you count his lone postseason snag) went for either a first down or a touchdown. “He's everything and that much more than I hoped he would be, and I had tremendously high hopes for him, and I think that he's gonna be a huge part of what we're gonna do for years to come” #Rams HC Sean McVay had a lot to say about Terrance Ferguson in his end-of-season presser https://t.co/VNYfaW5hgp pic.twitter.com/6AWaAReYoX — The Coachspeak Index (@CoachspeakIndex) February 12, 2026 The upside here shouldn’t be a surprise to anyone at this point, as Ferguson is getting plenty of attention in league circles. Last week, in a camp notebook from the campus of Loyola Marymount University, Sports Illustrated’s Albert Breer had a glowing review of the second-year tight end. “Terrance Ferguson has had a fantastic offseason,” Breer wrote. “He is now proving to be a guy who can play all over the formation and looks like he could be a force after the catch, showing why the Rams coveted him in the 2025 draft and now believe he could grow into one of the NFL’s best tight ends.” That’s a lofty goal but again, not an especially surprising one for Ferguson. Consider how dangerous he was while playing an unrefined game as a rookie. According to NFL Pro/Next Gen Stats, Ferguson led all qualified tight ends last season with 17.6 air yards per attempt, an average more than six yards per attempt higher than the second-place finisher. L.A. wants to push the ball downfield to Ferguson, and they did it to great albeit limited success (remember the conversion stat from above), both because he only played 39% of the team’s offensive snaps last year and because he only caught 40% of his targets. The Athletic Football Show also named Ferguson one of its second-year X-factors in an episode this past week, and it was a gush-fest over the young Ram. “Opportunity is going to be a big problem with this because they do have so many capable tight ends,” co-host Dave Helman said, “but Terrance Ferguson is probably your best bet to become basically ‘Wide Receiver 3’ in that offense, and if he does it could be really, really fun. Not that the Rams need the help, but I would enjoy watching it.” Helman is right that opportunities will be spread thin in a room that also includes the do-it-all “Y” Colby Parkinson , the long-time contributor Tyler Higbee and another high-upside rookie in Max Klare. But if Ferguson is indeed the skeleton key who can open new doors for this Rams offense, they’re going to find a way to get him on the field. They’ve got superstars. They’ve got an offense that’s already explosive (fourth in explosive pass rate last season, in fact). But another step forward for Ferguson this year could be the piece that propels Los Angeles back to the head of the pack this season.
author: Brendan Dzwierzynski

title: Why Puka Nacua hired a new agent
summary: Puka Nacua is showing up for the Los Angeles Rams but he, like many around the United States, wants to be paid for his services and he wants to be paid market value. Right now, Nacua is on his rookie deal and considering his stats, he’s well below what many other wide receivers who have […]
full_text: LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA - AUGUST 1: Puka Nacua #12 of the Los Angeles Rams points during training camp at Loyola Marymount University on August 1, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo by Ric Tapia/Getty Images) | Getty Images Puka Nacua is showing up for the Los Angeles Rams but he, like many around the United States, wants to be paid for his services and he wants to be paid market value. Right now, Nacua is on his rookie deal and considering his stats, he’s well below what many other wide receivers who have done less are making. So, Nacua has changed agencies from Athletes First to Win Sports Group, and considering what they were able to help get Zay Flowers (who’s a fine receiver, but not Puka Nacua), Nacua will likely be earning a massive deal. Nacua getting a new deal will likely be a surprise to no one, but how much he makes? That might be a shocker. Rams training camp updates: Puka Nacua explains why he changed agents (latimes.com) “With a massive payday potentially looming as he enters the final year of his rookie contract, Rams star receiver Puka Nacua recently changed agents. Nacua, who had been represented by Athletes First, signed with Win Sports Group, which negotiated huge deals for Seattle Seahawks receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba and Baltimore Ravens receiver Zay Flowers. “It was something for me, looking at the offseason and where I feel like I’ve been at in this past year,” Nacua said of the change. “Trying to reset and be able to refocus and reprioritize some of the things that I feel like are best for me. “I’m grateful to feel like I have a team supporting me in all facets.” Nacua led the NFL in receptions last season and was voted an All-Pro. The 2023 fifth-round draft pick is due to earn about $5.8 million this season, according to Overthecap.com .“ People around the NFL think Aaron Donald will be back with Rams. If you’ve been paying ANY attention to the NFL, then you’ve heard that the Los Angeles Rams are Super Bowl favorites and you’ve heard they traded for Myles Garrett (and some others), AND you’ve heard that Aaron Donald may come out of retirement to join the Rams. If you’ve been paying more attention than JUST ANY attention than EVERY person who talks about this subject is expecting Donald to be back with the Rams, and they are expecting this team to be must-watch television. If you’ve checked NFL news even once a day then you should know all the above information, yet, no one knows for sure that Donald will be back, but at this point, the horse seems out of the barn. It’s expected (dare I say a known unknown?) that Donald will be back and if he’s not, it will be a sigh of relief for 31 out of 32 teams, and maybe a bit of disappointment for the Rams, their fans and the talking heads who are just trying to stay afloat until the season kicks off. So MUCH Donald news, so little time. Just kidding, we have plenty of time! But remember, the season will here before we know it. Enjoy this last month. The NFL is coming. Thank YOU for checking out Turf Show Times and happy Friday! We made it! Aaron Donald decision updates: Live rumors, news on Rams return (usatoday) “The Rams ‘ Infinity Gauntlet is missing but one stone. Whether Los Angeles is able to procure a gem in Aaron Donald to fill out its defense should be answered in short order. The 35-year-old former Rams defensive star is looking to possibly drop the “former” from that distinction. His most recent act of testing the waters was working out with the Rams on Wednesday, Aug. 5. While no decision has been made on whether Donald will remain retired, Wednesday’s workout through camp required the team to inform the league, as the three-time player of the year used official team gear and a helmet, according to Adam Schefter .“ Trent McDuffie getting used to being with the Rams and taking in their trades. Trent McDuffie was blown away by Rams’ reaction to Verse-Garrett trade (ramswire) “And it’s not lost on players in Los Angeles just how important and valuable Verse was to the team. That showed in the meeting room after Sean McVay shared the news of Verse being traded for Garrett. Trent McDuffie opened up about that meeting on “Bussin’ With The Boys” with Taylor Lewan, calling it one of his favorite moments with the Rams so far. Not because the team landed an all-world player in Garrett, but because of how everyone reacted to losing Verse.“ Always players to keep an eye out for, looking at your Grant Stuard. ‘He’s a Tasmanian devil’: Rams’ new LB bringing the energy to camp (ramswire) “One of the more underrated and intriguing signings from what was a star-studded offseason, Grant Stuard has made it clear that he takes nothing for granted and is a player who has earned every ounce of football success he’s experienced. The final pick in the 2021 NFL Draft, Stuard has used his brazenness and physicality to carve out a long-term special teams role, while being a strong depth linebacker. This is critical as the Los Angeles Rams needed to fill gaps at both positions this offseason, with their special teams being a massive point of concern.“ Rams hope to sure up their secondary (you know that). Rams Bet Big On McDuffie, Watson For Super Bowl Chase (athlonsports) “After a costly secondary sank their 2025 title run, the Los Angeles Rams added Trent McDuffie and Jaylen Watson, entering 2026 as Super Bowl favorites.” Myles Garrett is getting used to being on the Rams. Myles Garrett on his first Rams Training Camp, breaking the sack record, goals for this season & more | Inside Rams Camp (therams.com) “Los Angeles Rams defensive end Myles Garrett joins Camryn Irwin and J.B. Long for an episode of Inside Rams Camp presented by Community America Credit Union. On the show, Myles talks about his first training camp in Los Angeles, building chemistry with his new teammates, breaking the sack record and hoping to break it again, goals for the 2026 season, and more!” Some betting news . NFL Futures Trends to Know as the 2026 NFL Preseason Begins (hardrock.bet) “Many believe Los Angeles has assembled a superteam capable of making another championship run. The Rams lead all 32 teams with 16.38% of the total bets and have also generated the highest handle in the market at 12.78% , giving them the strongest overall betting support to win the Lombardi Trophy. “Josh Allen and the Buffalo Bills are also looking to finally capture a championship and are drawing notable attention with the second-highest handle . Joe Burrow and the Cincinnati Bengals are right behind them with the third-highest handle despite generating just 3.34% of bets to win Super Bowl 61 and coming off a 6-11 season in 2025. Chris Shula would be “really excited” about Aaron Donald returning (if he does) (nbcsports) “Obviously, I’d be really excited about that,” defensive coordinator Chris Shula told reporters on Wednesday regarding the possibility of Donald coming back. “You’re getting one of the best players of all time. I’ve had a great history with him. I was here in ’17, coaching other positions with him. I know what a great guy he is, what a hard worker he is, and what he would mean to this defense. But at the same time, we’re going to coach the guys who are here and if he decides to come back, that’d be great.” Donald took the next step earlier this week, with a “tryout” during (we’re told) a day off for players at training camp. Shula wasn’t present for the session that was far less about evaluating Donald and much more about Donald seeing how he felt — with the goal of finding out if he can get back to being the great player he was.“ New Insider Report on Aaron Donald Puts Rams Rival On Notice (heavy.com) “Florio again said Donald’s recent workout at the Rams’ facilities was more for his benefit than the team’s. But Florio also explained that in addition to anticipating a potential answer from Donald this coming week, the Rams already have a plan for him to play Week 1. That is, as it has been, if Donald feels he is up to it.…

title: Raiders Training Camp: Michael Mayer will be a vital part of the 2026 offense
summary: HENDERSON, Nevada — The Las Vegas Raiders drafted Michael Mayer to be their star tight end in 2023. However, everything changed the next season when the Raiders drafted Brock Bowers, who became the starting tight end and reduced Mayer’s role in the offense. It led Mayer to struggle off the field and lose some confidence. […]
full_text: HENDERSON, NEVADA - JULY 29: Michael Mayer #87 of the Las Vegas Raiders runs through a drill during the first practice of the team's training camp at the Las Vegas Raiders Headquarters/Intermountain Health Performance Center on July 29, 2026 in Henderson, Nevada. (Photo by Ian Maule/Getty Images) | Getty Images HENDERSON, Nevada — The Las Vegas Raiders drafted Michael Mayer to be their star tight end in 2023. However, everything changed the next season when the Raiders drafted Brock Bowers, who became the starting tight end and reduced Mayer’s role in the offense. It led Mayer to struggle off the field and lose some confidence. After a small bounce-back season in 2025, the former Notre Dame tight end is expected to have a bigger role with Klint Kubiak as the head coach. His relationship with Brock Bowers has grown as well. The two will be seen on the field together on plenty of looks. Mayer thinks the tandem can grow into one of the best in the NFL. “Two big threats that can both block really well; I think it is going to be an interesting season in terms of that just have to keep working hard, keep our heads down. Klint has a plan for us, and we will do our best to follow it.” Mayer was featured during practice and had a long touchdown during the team session. He followed it up with a big catch over the middle using his size to hold off Taron Johnson. Bowers and Mayer could be the next great tight end tandem if the Raiders find a way to execute on offense. Other Training Camp Notes : -Kirk Cousins and Maxx Crosby got into a scuffle after Crosby hit Cousins in the arm for the second time. Jonah Laulu and Caleb Rogers had an altercation as well. -Mendoza looked sharp all practice and displayed his ability in the red zone by splitting the defense with a beautiful slant for a touchdown. He then had a great pass over the middle in team period and displayed anticipation throughout practice. -Malcolm Koonce got his chance to shine with Kwity Paye and Keyron Crawford missing practice. Koonce bull-rushed Jack Bech into the ground and was constantly being disruptive. -Malik Benson continues to shine, but it was a big day for Tre Tucker. Tucker caught a great back shoulder from Cousins and shook Eric Stokes in the red zone for a touchdown. Tucker looked prime to silence the naysayers. -Two unsung players of the day were Gary Smith III and JJ Pegues. Pegues got run with the ones at nose tackle and was explosive all practice. He did leave early with an injury. -Overall, the defense is dominating so far during training camp, which might have led to the longer practice today. Usually a two-hour practice, it went about two and a half hours.
author: Marcus Johnson

title: Raiders training camp showing encouraging signs of a player-led defense
summary: If there’s ever a time for Las Vegas Raiders defenders to play fast and make mistakes, it’s training camp. Especially with the team no longer participating in what safeties coach Matt Robinson called “the underwear Olympics” phase of camp since the team putting on pads this past Monday and engaging in some “real football”. “It’s […]
full_text: HENDERSON, NEVADA - JULY 29: Quay Walker #7 of the Las Vegas Raiders stretches during the first practice of the team's training camp at the Las Vegas Raiders Headquarters/Intermountain Health Performance Center on July 29, 2026 in Henderson, Nevada. (Photo by Ian Maule/Getty Images) | Getty Images If there’s ever a time for Las Vegas Raiders defenders to play fast and make mistakes, it’s training camp. Especially with the team no longer participating in what safeties coach Matt Robinson called “the underwear Olympics” phase of camp since the team putting on pads this past Monday and engaging in some “real football”. “It’s like you want them to feel comfortable but this is the time for mistakes,” Raiders defensive coordinator Rob Leonard said when asked if he’s seen the if you make mistakes, make them while playing fast mantra he’s preached about. “We talk about in the offseason was a lot of what I would call lecture of like these are our techniques and this is exactly what we’re asking for.” Leonard, in his first season as the defensive boss under head coach Klint Kubiak after earning the promotion from defensive line coach and defensive run game coordinator, is neophyte in his position much like the man helming the Silver & Black ship is. Unlike Kubiak, Leonard doesn’t have a recent Lombardi Trophy on his resume — the Raiders head honcho joined the Raiders shortly after orchestrating the Seattle Seahawks Super Bowl-winning 2025 offense — but that doesn’t mean the defensive coordinator hasn’t earned the attention and respect from players under his charge. Heralded as a player’s coach who excels at creating bonds with locker room vernacular while maintaining a highly technical teaching style, Leonard is right there in the mud with his players during drills and practices all throughout the offseason. And like the head coach who tabbed him as the new defensive coordinator, Leonard is adamant in his philosophy of a player-centric and collaborative environment. “But now, I’m trying to press a player-led defense,” Leonard said. “I want them to have control and confidence to get in and out of whatever we’re doing out there and make a decision. We’ll talk about as you learn the strengths and weaknesses of the decision you make and why we’re trying to do that. I think the why is a big thing that we’re emphasizing right now.” Las Vegas Raiders Training Camp Video #6. Courtesy of, On SI pic.twitter.com/YWl65focIV — Hondo Carpenter (@HondoCarpenter) August 3, 2026 Training camp is showcasing encouraging signs that a player-led defense is forming just as Leonard wants. This includes what you’d normally expect from an NFL team, such as: Accountability and veterans paving the way as lead-by-example types. There’s growing communication that’ll be instrumental to the defense’s overall success. The more they continue to do so deep into the regular season, the better. And a growing culture where there’s no ego, teammates are actively helping each other and holding one another accountable for errors. But it’s the vocal communication and on-field ownership which resulted in an intriguing moment where Leonard himself was told to skedaddle from the huddle. “Command. Confidence,” Leonard began when asked about what’s stood out regarding prized free agent addition Nakobe Dean, ‘Robbie, get out of my huddle. I got it.’ I want to get up in there and start up, but that’s not reality of how the game’s played. Just leadership. It feels good to have that at the Mike linebacker.” Once Leonard made that known at the podium during his media availability post training camp practice, it didn’t take long for other Raiders to be asked about Dean telling Leonard get out of here, I got this. Fellow free agent-addition and linebacker Quay Walker and cornerback Eric Stokes — who both went to Georgia alongside Dean — had interesting responses to said query. Walker was pragmatic about it. “Not quite, because I don’t think the coaches really got in the huddle,” Walker began,. when asked if he’s seen something like a defensive coordinator getting kicked out of the huddle by a middle linebacker. “We didn’t have the mics in college, so all of us had to look to the sideline and get the call. They were sending them, so it’s kind of different here. He’s probably kicking them out because in the game they’re not going to be able to get in the huddle. So that’s probably the reason why he’s doing that.” Stokes had a hyped up response. “Heck yeah, that’s exactly what we want for our middle linebacker, our Mike in the middle,” Stokes said when asked if Dean has always been a take-command type. “Like we want you to take control. We want you to be that. Like man, nah, the coach ain’t gonna be out there on the field with us, so don’t even be out here on the field with us during practice. Like let us run the show.” #Raiders DC Rob Leonard on what he’s seen from Nakobe Dean “Command, confidence…leadership, it feels good to have that at the Mike linebacker” He even told us Dean said: “Robbie get outta my huddle, I got it.” — Jesse Merrick – Silver & Black Sports Network (@JesseSBSN) July 30, 2026 A few days later, turns out, his fellow Bulldogs nailed it with their responses. “When you’re the Mike (linebacker), you want to hear your coordinator talk,” Dean began when describing the mentality and thought process of throwing Leonard out of the huddle. “You want to hear him talk to you. You want to hear how he’s going to call the calls. You want to hear if he is going to just say the call and get off the mic, or is he going to give you checks and everything. “So, you don’t want him just in the huddle making the call. You want the team to hear you too. I mean, I’m from Mississippi — I don’t have trouble anymore — so I’ve had trouble before with guys not understanding some of the things that I say. So, I want the guys to hear me and hear how I make the play calls and everything too.” That’s the type of ownership and player-led nature Leonard wants and it’s rooting itself and growing in Las Vegas. Beyond the standard setter-type veterans like edge rusher Maxx Crosby, Dean, Walker, left tackle Kolton Miller, tight end Brock Bowers, to name a few, newcomer Taron Johnson is showcasing Leonard’s desired confidence and command. Acquired via trade with the Buffalo Bills (Las Vegas received the veteran cornerback and a 2026 seventh-round pick (traded during draft) in exchange for a 2026 sixth-round pick), Johnson is slated to man the integral nickel cornerback role providing physicality, coverage, and command covering the slot. “Same thing like with Nakobe; confidence, anticipation, command,” Leonard said about Johnson. “Even if we’re not right, he’s going to make a call and go. Guys listen to him. Physicality, just honestly, he’s like an energy bus guy. I love those guys, Energizer Bunny, he’s one of those.” The Raiders are prepping for a 2026 campaign with a new coaching staff and renewed vigor. But we’ve seen this song and dance before. The excitement and hope giving way to dejection and misery. It’s on Leonard and his defense to make the encouraging signs we’ve seen so far in training camp into tangible progress and production Week 1 of the regular season and beyond.
author: Ray Aspuria

title: Las Vegas Raiders Breakout Candidates
summary: The 2026 NFL season is nearly in full swing, with the Las Vegas Raiders starting training camp & eventually they’ll be playing their first pre-season game coming up very quickly. The NFL always sees players hit their strides, breakout, and become core players on their rosters especially young players who have made strides and are […]
full_text: LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - NOVEMBER 17: Tre Tucker #1 of the Las Vegas Raiders scores a touchdown against the Dallas Cowboys during the fourth quarter at Allegiant Stadium on November 17, 2025 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo by Candice Ward/Getty Images) | Getty Images The 2026 NFL season is nearly in full swing, with the Las Vegas Raiders starting training camp & eventually they’ll be playing their first pre-season game coming up very quickly. The NFL always sees players hit their strides, breakout, and become core players on their rosters especially young players who have made strides and are set to see more snaps in different schemes. The Raiders offense and defensive coaching staff’s have been extremely turned over, and as a result, there will be opportunities for coaches that weren’t present earlier in their careers. All that in mind, my potential breakout candidates are below: WR Jalen Nailor Nailor is coming to Las Vegas after serving as the main WR3 and at times 2nd receiver in the Vikings system where he logged 57 receptions, 858 yards, and 10 touchdowns over the last two seasons. The former 6th rounder has history with Klint Kubiak and is arguably the best receiver in the Raiders room. Similar to Tre Tucker, Nailor has a chance to explode in an offense that will give him opportunities with the ball in his hands, and also scheme him open. Nailor isn’t a prototypical X receiver, and works best in the Z/Slot but he’s an explosive receiver, who has a ton of natural speed especially in his start/stop abilities. There’s been moments of Nailor showing the ability to be a consistent 1000 yard receiver, and he has a good chance in Las Vegas. 61 yards with some stiff arms for Jalen Nailor! BALvsMIN on FOX/FOX One https://t.co/HkKw7uXVnt pic.twitter.com/9zSE12OqME — NFL (@NFL) November 9, 2025 WR Tre Tucker I’ve been a big fan of Tre Tucker for the last few years and I think 2026 will be the year everything comes to mold. To start, Tucker is coming off his best season in 2025 with 57 receptions, 696 yards, and five touchdowns. Additionally, Tucker should see his chance to play in an offense that will allow him to work with the ball in his hands, work intermediate threat, but also be the true top off the defense option. Tucker needs to improve on his drops, but he’s shown the speed, improved route running, and contested catch ability that can make him a capable WR2 in the NFL. Heading into a career year, and a new offense (the fourth of his career) Tucker will also have the best QB play he’s had in his NFL tenure. DT Tonka Hemingway Hemingway saw his rookie season filled with ups and downs, where he logged 4 sacks, 5 TFL, and 9 tackles along with 7 QB hits and a PBU. Hemingway saw inconsistencies in his pass rush, largely needing to improve his pass rush moves, and he was a raw prospect in that regard coming out of South Carolina. That said, Hemingway is an ultra athlete, he’s able to consistently use his first step and second step moves to get upfield and get past the offensive line. Additionally, Hemingway is strong in his lower half and converts speed to power with a great bull rush. There’s issues as a run defender, where Hemingway has never been good stemming back to South Carolina, but the Raiders should put him in a spot to be a capable pass rusher and he does have double 8+ sack potential with improved pass rush moves. Tonka Hemingway is a guy to keep an eye on as #Raiders camp rolls on. He’s been getting work with the ones alongside Adam Butler… so the opportunity to earn a bigger role is there for him as he enters his second season. pic.twitter.com/EetgeFfi5N — Jesse Merrick – Silver & Black Sports Network (@JesseSBSN) July 31, 2026 DT Thomas Booker IV Booker is similar to Hemingway, he’s an ultra athlete but he’s bigger, and likely a bit stronger as well. Booker’s pass rush moves need improvement, but he’s shown an ability to add a club/swipe and he has an elite swim move as well. Booker didn’t record a sack in 2025, but he created 7 sacks for fellow defensive lineman, including 2 of Hemingway’s 4. Booker is likely to see similar, or increased snaps this season depending on Adam Butler’s potential regression and Tonka Hemingway’s development. Booker is an adequate run defender, but he’s best in pass rush situations using his strength and athleticism to get upfield quickly and flush quarterbacks into uncomfortable situations as he did last season. LB Segun Olubi Olubi has just 32 tackles, an interception, and a FR in his 141 NFL snaps which include just 28 over the last two seasons. Olubi has been a standout on special teams, and there’s no question on his ability to provide for the Raiders in that regard this season where the expectation is likely at least one turnover and one blocked kick. The Raiders have relatively limited LB depth behind Quay Walker & Nakobe Dean (honorable mention breakout candidate if he stays healthy) who both need to stay healthy, but have a history of missing games. If one goes down, the Raiders are likely to ask Olubi to step up into a WILL or SAM role with the non injured linebackers and/or Tommy Eichenberg playing the MIKE role. Olubi has shown a good understanding of the run game, instincts in coverage, and he moves well with sideline to sideline range. He’s just 27 and around the age of NFL breakouts for linebackers. This is likely a long shot, but if an injury occurs you could possibly feel comfortable with Olubi as a depth option. First NFL interception for Segun Olubi! 👏 📺 CBS pic.twitter.com/AB18yFNbGT — Indianapolis Colts (@Colts) November 5, 2023 CB Hezekiah Masses It’s hard to call a rookie a breakout, but Masses has a chance. The 5th rounder has been working with the first team CBs along side Eric Stokes, Darien Porter, and Jermod McCoy indicating that the Raiders are likely to rotate their secondary heavily (as they should). Masses has added weight which was necessary due to his biggest flaws being at the catch point and a lack of strength in the run game. Masses is an incredible athlete, has elite ball skills, and he’s a good mover in coverage. Masses logged 5 interceptions, and 18 PBU in just 13 games last year while allowing a 55.8 QBR. Masses has among the best, if not the best, pure ball skills in the Raiders secondary and if he can find consistency at the catch point, maintain his natural instincts, and play patient there’s room for a breakout rookie season. TE Michael Mayer I’ll be quick because Mayer has always been mentioned a breakout, there’s a great shot that Mayer will see a career high in snaps this season as the inline TE with Brock Bowers split into an H-Back, or slot role. Increased snaps should improve Mayer’s total receiving line, and he should also figure to be a big player in the red zone. Mayer is a top run blocker, and that alone will get him paid well this off-season, but improve his receiving film could go a long way as well. Klint Kubiak’s offense has lived heavily out of 12 personnel, and a large part of that offense can be implemented with Bowers and Mayer.

title: Pro Football Hall of Fame: Which Dolphins players should be enshrined?
summary: The Pro Football Hall of Fame will hold their 2026 enshrinement ceremony on Saturday, adding five members to the ultimate individual honor given to a player, coach, or contributor. Quarterback Drew Brees, running back Roger Craig, wide receiver Larry Fitzgerald, linebacker Luke Kuechly, and kicker Adam Vinatieri will be presented their gold jackets and have […]
full_text: IRVING, TX - NOVEMBER 25: Tackle Richmond Webb #of the Miami Dolphins looks to block against the Dallas Cowboys at Texas Stadium on November 25, 1993 in Irving, Texas. The Dolphins defeated the Cowboys 16-14. (Photo by Joseph Patronite/Getty Images) The Pro Football Hall of Fame will hold their 2026 enshrinement ceremony on Saturday, adding five members to the ultimate individual honor given to a player, coach, or contributor. Quarterback Drew Brees, running back Roger Craig, wide receiver Larry Fitzgerald, linebacker Luke Kuechly, and kicker Adam Vinatieri will be presented their gold jackets and have their bronze busts revealed before they are emplaced into the Hall of Fame in Canton, Ohio, making them official members of the game’s immortals. Who should be next for the Dolphins? There are a few names who probably should be in the Hall of Fame, a few who could flirt with consideration, and my personal dark horse who I think should land in Canton at some point, but probably never will. Miami Dolphins Hall of Famers The Miami Dolphins have 11 players or coaches who became legends with the team and earned a spot in Canton. Nick Buoniconti, linebacker – 1969-1974, 1976 Larry Csonka, fullback – 1968-1974, 1979 Bob Griese, quarterback – 1967-1980 Jim Langer, center – 1970-1979 Larry Little, guard – 1969-1980 Dan Marino, quarterback – 1983-1999 Don Shula, head coach – 1970-1995 Dwight Stephenson, center – 1980-1987 Jason Taylor, defensive end – 1997-2007, 2009, 2011 Zach Thomas, linebacker – 1996-2007 Paul Warfield, wide receiver – 1970-1974 In addition to the Dolphins’ legends above, there are several other members of the team, either as players, coaches, or executives, who have made it to the Hall of Fame, but are probably better known for their time with another franchise. They include: Bobby Beathard – Washington GM (Dolphins Director of Player Personnel 1972-1977) Cris Carter – Minnesota Vikings wide receiver (Dolphins wide receiver 2002) Jimmy Johnson – Dallas Cowboys Head Coach (Dolphins Head coach 1996-1999) Bill Parcells – New York Giants/New England Patriots/New York Jets/Dallas Cowboys Head Coach (Dolphins Executive Vice President of Football Operations 2008-2010) Junior Seau – San Diego Chargers linebacker (Dolphins linebacker 2003-2005) Thurman Thomas – Buffalo Bills running back (Dolphins running back 2000) George Young – New York Giants GM / NFL Senior VP of Football Operations (Dolphins Director of Personnel and Pro Scouting 1975 – 1978) Who should be Miami’s next Hall of Famer? Taking a look at players, coaches, and executives who made their major contributions in the game while they were with the Dolphins, there are four names who could be considered snubs for enshrinement. Richmond Webb, tackle (Miami Dolphins 1990-2000, Cincinnati Bengals 2001-2002) Webb’s biggest hurdle in making the Hall of Fame is probably the era in which he played. Not because of any changes the NFL has made, but because he is was the blind side protector for Hall of Fame quarterback Dan Marino – whose quick release was a highlight of his game, but can be used against Webb. That said, Webb was a four-time All-Pro selection (two first team, two second team) and seven-time Pro Bowl selection. He was named to the NFL All-Decade Team for the 1990s, and is the only tackle from the team who has not been inducted into the Hall of Fame. Webb played 184 games in the NFL, including his final two years when he played with the Cincinnati Bengals, starting all but one contest. He went toe-to-toe with Hall of Fame defensive end Bruce Smith twice a year every year in the Dolphins and Bills rivalry – making an edge rusher versus a left tackle a must watch matchup. Smith’s 0.61 sacks per game average against the Dolphins – and Webb – was the lowest of his career against any team he saw twice a season. Webb was a semi-finalist for the Hall of Fame in 2025 and 2026 Mark Clayton, wide receiver (Miami Dolphins 1983-1992, Green Bay Packers 1993) Like Webb, Clayton may be stuck on the wrong side of Canton’s cut line simply because he played with Marino. A five-time Pro Bowl selection and two-time NFL touchdown pass leader, Clayton – as well as his fellow Dolphins receiver Mark Duper – was integral to Marino’s success as a passer and the Dolphins’ success on offense. He caught 582 passes during his career, including the 32 he caught in his final season with the Packers, and he tallied 8,974 yards with 84 touchdowns in 158 career games. His 84 touchdown catches ranks 23rd all time, with 16 of those ahead of him already inducted and four either currently active or recently retired and likely to be inducted once eligible. He is tied with Hall of Fame receiver Fred Biletnikoff for 76th all time in receiving yards. Clayton has moved past his eligibility for the modern era vote process, so if he were to ever receive his gold jacket, it would have to come from the senior committee’s consideration. Bob Kuechenberg, offensive line (Miami Dolphins 1970-1984) The road for Kuechenberg to claim a spot in Canton seems like a steep, uphill climb. Despite played for 15 seasons, primarily at left guard, there seems to be an idea that the 1972 Dolphins undefeated team is already over-represented in the Hall of Fame, especially with Langer and Little representing the linemen from that era. Somehow being one of the best in a group of elite linemen has hurt the argument for Kuechenberg. Kuechenberg played 194 games for the Dolphins, holding the franchise record for more than a decade until Marino surpassed him. As an offensive lineman, he missed just five games from 1970 through 1983. He was a six-time Pro Bowl selection and two-time First-Team All-Pro selection with another All-Pro selection to the Second-Team. He was a finalist for the Hall of Fame eight times, but never made it through the final round of voting. Like Clayton, it would be up to the senior committee to add Kuechenberg to the Hall of Fame. Bills Arnsparger, coach (Miami Dolphins defensive coordinator 1970-1973, 1976-1983; New York Giants head coach 1974-1976) If there is any coach who should be in the Hall of Fame for his work as an assistant, it is Arnsparger. When Don Shula was named the head coach of the Dolphins, he brought along Arnsparger, promoting him from the Baltimore Colts’ defensive linemen coach to the Dolphins’ defensive coordinator. Two years later, Miami was in the Super Bowl, then returned for two championships, in large part thanks to Arnsparger’s system leading to the “No Name Defense.” After an unsuccessful stint as the head coach of the Giants, Arnsparger returned to the Dolphins and once again built a dominating defense. This time, the “Killer B” defense would lead Miami back to the Super Bowl, though they could not come away with the title. He left the Dolphins after the 1983 season to become the head coach at LSU, then became the athletic director at Florida until 1992 when he returned to the NFL as the San Diego Chargers’ defensive coordinator. The Chargers made a run to the Super Bowl in 1994 – played in Miami – with Arnsparger’s defense, though they did not win. He retired after the Super Bowl due to cancer issues. The Hall of Fame keeps considering Arnsparger, including for the 2026 class, but he did not make it to the semifinalist round. Hall of Fame bubble watch These players are probably not destined to land in Canton, but they had really good careers and could be that bubble player that hangs around for a while. Mark Duper, wide receiver Sam Madison, cornerback Patrick Surtain, cornerback Cameron Wake, edge Ricky Williams, running back Of that list, Wake could eventually find the momentum to become a strong candidate. Wake played 11 seasons, 10 with the Dolphins. After going undrafted in 2005 and a brief, pre-training camp stint as a linebacker with the New York Giants, Wake moved to the Canadian Football League in 2007 and switched to defensive end. A star was born, and the Dolphins made sure to land him…

title: Vikings Training Camp Notes: 8/7 Edition
summary: The rain stopped and later the sun came out for the Minnesota Vikings training camp practice today, which was in full pads. It wasn’t nearly as intense as the padded practice on Wednesday, nor was it really as eventful, but nevertheless some tid bits here and there can be gleaned from the performance. So, with […]
full_text: The rain stopped and later the sun came out for the Minnesota Vikings training camp practice today, which was in full pads. It wasn’t nearly as intense as the padded practice on Wednesday, nor was it really as eventful, but nevertheless some tid bits here and there can be gleaned from the performance. So, with that, let’s get into it. Quarterback Competition This was another practice where Kyler Murray got most of the first-team reps, which has been the trend for several practices now. But today J.J. McCarthy had the better practice. Today McCarthy was near the high-end of the range of performance we’ve seen from him in training camp going back to last year. He didn’t exceed the high-end of his range into higher territory which would be considered improvement, but he looked sharp on most of his throws, but nearly all of them would be considered of the more routine variety. He did have a couple nice intermediate completions in team drills and looked more decisive on more of his short throws. He did have a deep attempt down the sideline to Gavin Bartholomew which was slightly overthrown, and he had a couple other misfires as well- and a couple sacks- so it wasn’t a perfect day by any means, but he seemed a bit more comfortable in the pocket. For Kyler Murray, he was closer to the low-end of the range we’ve seen since the start of training camp and stretching into the offseason program. He overshot a couple passes, had a couple would-be sacks, and otherwise mostly shorter, routine completions. He had a deep, more line-drive touchdown pass negated either by a would-be sack or a whistle, but Tai Felton was super wide open and it appeared the defense had stopped so it didn’t count. Similarly, he had an interception following a whistle- perhaps an offsides or something like that where some players stopped and the play was negated. He also had another jump-ball type throw to Justin Jefferson in single coverage against Byron Murphy Jr., which was a good throw but went threw Jefferson’s hands- but the play was also negated by an offensive pass interference call against Jefferson for pushing off- which he clearly did. He held the ball it bit longer again today looking for deeper passes that mostly didn’t materialize. Overall McCarthy looked sharper today than Murray, who is also celebrating his birthday, in a day that was almost entirely routine throws in 11-on-11 team drills. Probably a day where coverage won more than anything and probably not a practice that moves the needle much in the quarterback competition. But give McCarthy his due for operating more at the top end of his range. Lastly, I didn’t track the snap counts, but I thought Carson Wentz particularly got a few more reps than normal today- Brosmer maybe a couple more too. Neither one get more than a few reps in team drills normally so this isn’t saying much, but worth mentioning. Good Day for Brett Thorson Specialists got some work today in team drills and more extensive punt drills and Brett Thorson took advantage of his opportunities. First, he had three reps as a holder in team drills, with the offensive having just one play and then a punt or field goal try. Thorson was holder for three field goal attempts by Will Reichard and he made all three of them. That was good for Thorson as he wasn’t a holder in college and whether he beats Johnny Hekker or not may hinge on his holding ability. But Thorson also had some booming punts. It was difficult to tell exactly the yardage, but one looked to go about sixty yards and was caught near the sideline and another was longer than that with good location by the sideline too. Thorson was more mixed when it came to avoiding touchbacks, as was Johnny Hekker. Overall, if the Vikings feel comfortable/confident in Thorson’s holding ability, I think his punting ability will overshadow the aging Hekker and could win him the punter/holder job. Lots of Rotation One thing I haven’t said specifically before is that there is a lot of rotation throughout team drills- a bit more than I remember in previous years- particularly on the defensive side. Defensive interior linemen in particular are rotated about every two plays it seems, but linebackers and defensive backs have a regular rotation as well. Offensively, the first team offensive line does not rotate, but all the skill positions do to some extent. And the second team offensive line has some rotation, and skill positions more so. Overall not super unusual, but there is a bit more rotation than normal going on this year. That’s probably a good sign for younger guys trying to make the roster. Other Miscellaneous Notes This may not be breaking news, but Levi Drake-Rodriguez is kind of a dude. He seems to be taking on a bit of a leadership role amongst the defensive tackles, who are mostly quieter personalities and/or rookies, along with Jalen Redmond as the best player. As the two rookie defensive tackles Big Citrus and Caleb Banks ramp up, a lot will hinge on LDR in terms of how good the defensive interior is, especially early-on this season. Tyrion Ingram-Dawkins too. But LDR looks like he is ready to take a step up this year. Offensive line coach Keith Carter, along with receivers coach Keenan McCardell, are the most active position coaches for the Vikings. Early on in practice today, Carter had already soaked his t-shirt in sweat and he is seemingly always out there coaching up his players, even between plays in team drills, and barking out instructions in individual position group drills. Defensive Line coach Ryan Nielson shows a very individualized, technical approach with his group, spending more time with each player in drills with very detailed coaching. After looking repeatedly at my roster list and wondering why Chaz Chambliss (listed as #32) was playing defensive back, and also noting that he is now Black, I discovered that Jamal Adams had switched numbers and was taking snaps at safety. He played both box and deep safety at times. Apparently both Jay Ward and Jakobe Thomas were not participating in team drills today. Where Adams is positioned is something to monitor going forward. Jakobe Thomas hasn’t been particularly impressive so far- he may be swimming a bit in learning the defense. Of the longshots to make the roster at wide receiver, Dontae Fleming has been the most impressive. He had a couple nice grabs today, but also a drop. He seems like he’s got more ability to separate than the others. Run Game Notes The Vikings have been clamping down more on the no video policy they’ve had for years for training camp attendees, to keep secret new wrinkles in their scheme from getting out to opposing teams. Offensively, there may be greater reason for that this year as there may be more evolution in scheme than in previous years, particularly in the run game. I did a piece on potential new wrinkles in the offensive scheme a couple weeks ago, and it appears that some of that is showing up on the practice field. The Frank Smith influence is evident in some of the new looks in the run game in particular. But so far in training camp, the defense has had the upper hand in defending the run game as successful runs have been few and far between. Today there was a bit more success for the offense later in team drills, as a couple holes opened that Aaron Jones and Jordan Mason were able to exploit. And while Aaron Jones is still running exclusively with the first-team offense as expected, I wouldn’t be surprised if the Vikings lean more on Jordan Mason this season, even if Jones is healthy. Mason was the more efficient back last season for the Vikings, and he returned trimmer and looks more involved in the pass game too. Demond Claiborne and Max Bredeson were paired frequently with the second team offense on Wednesday and even had a couple reps with the first team, and I could see the Vikings hoping both of those players earn significant roles this season. I noticed both Claiborne and Mason working on their…
