title: Hard Knocks sheds light on why Cooper Kupp was never in danger of being a cap casualty
summary: During the 2025 regular season, and then in the immediate aftermath of the Seattle Seahawks thumping the New England Patriots 29-13 in Super Bowl LX, there was no shortage of fans calling for the team to move on from Cooper Kupp for salary cap reasons. The voices were loud and adamant that Kupp wasn’t worth […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - FEBRUARY 8: Cooper Kupp #10 of the Seattle Seahawks completes a catch against Marcus Jones #25 of the New England Patriots during the second quarter of the NFL Super Bowl LX football game at Levi's Stadium on February 08, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images During the 2025 regular season, and then in the immediate aftermath of the Seattle Seahawks thumping the New England Patriots 29-13 in Super Bowl LX, there was no shortage of fans calling for the team to move on from Cooper Kupp for salary cap reasons. The voices were loud and adamant that Kupp wasn’t worth the $17.5M cap hit his contract would carry in 2026, and his production did not justify the three-year, $45M contract he had signed in 2025. For many, it was a matter of when, not if, the Seahawks would move on from the veteran wideout during the offseason in spite of his on-field production and the fact that the structure of his contract made it abundantly clear he would be with the team in 2026. Just as an aside for those who were certain Kupp’s contract represents an overpay, here is a very basic plot of multi-year receiver contracts that had been signed as of this spring. Dots above the line represent overpays relative to production in the market, while dots below the line represent value signings in terms of production to average salary. It’s certainly simplistic and crude, but shows that it doesn’t take diving overly deep to come to the conclusion that Kupp’s contract represents a value in the current receiver market, even with his production far below what it was earlier in his career. full contract APY versus receiving production (in yards) the circled dots are Kupp and Shaheed pic.twitter.com/rutOd9OXMa — John P Gilbert (@JohnPGilbertNFL) March 10, 2026 With that said, in the days since the first episode of Hard Knocks multiple fans and observers have come to the realization of what Kupp brings to the team off the field in terms of leadership and knowledge. Cooper Kupp's leadership has been invaluable to the Seahawks 💯 Watch the first episode of Hard Knocks: Training Camp with the @seahawks now on @hbomax pic.twitter.com/sfBKla279J — NFL (@NFL) August 5, 2026 Brock & Salk touched on the subject the day after the premier episode aired. What did Hard Knocks showcase about the personality of the #Seahawks defense and offense? @BrockHuard & @TheMikeSalk share their biggest takeaways from the first episode 📽️🏈 (📺Full reaction: https://t.co/nZjVZOLjqW ) pic.twitter.com/GpBVoJnZ4I — Seattle Sports (@SeattleSports) August 5, 2026 Of course, this is nothing new to those who have been paying attention to Kupp throughout his career. He has long had a reputation as a hard worker and for possessing a very high football IQ. Specifically, glimpses of the level of his knowledge of the game came through from time to time, but perhaps no better moment shows the level at which he understands and processes the game better than this post game interview following a Week 13 win over the Jacksonville Jaguars in 2021. Cooper Kupp gave the most complex answer I’ve ever heard from a wide receiver 😂 pic.twitter.com/AyW4CpBnOf — Footballism (@FootbaIIism) December 7, 2021 Not only is that a highly detailed, in-depth technical answer, Kupp provided that answer in the moment without the benefit of film review. Perhaps making his recall of the play even more impressive is that he’s recalling these details in a post game interview and describing a play that took place with 11:51 left in the third quarter on the Los Angeles Rams first possession of the second half. Interestingly, though, according to Rams quarterback Matthew Stafford, Kupp provided this overly detailed and technical response specifically as an attempt to end the interview quickly. Cooper Kupp’s viral interview was actually just him pulling a veteran move @Mentos pic.twitter.com/hPTWsFu5yJ — New Heights (@newheightshow) March 12, 2025 Even if Kupp was simply using the response to bring the interview to a speedy conclusion, the reality is that his abilities to recognize, process and recall such details in real time without the benefit of film handy provide a huge amount of value to the team. In the modern NFL, where practice time is limited and contact between players and coaches heavily restricted during the offseason, having Kupp as a de facto gives the team a huge advantage in terms of what can be accomplished during the offseason. From understanding coverages to the intricacies of route running, Kupp can fill knowledge gaps and serve as a coach during the offseason at times when coaches aren’t allowed to coach due to the limitations set in place by the current collective bargaining agreement. Long story short, the team was never moving on from Kupp in the offseason, and the first episode of Hard Knocks shed a lot of light on why.

title: The Seahawks’ next evolution is about creating conflict on both sides of the ball
summary: The Seattle Seahawks have established a clear identity under Mike Macdonald. The next step is determining how that identity continues to evolve as Seattle enters another season with a roster increasingly suited to what Macdonald wants to accomplish. That was the focus of my latest episode of The Hawks Eye, where I was joined by […]
full_text: RENTON, WASHINGTON - JULY 25: Offensive Coordinator Brian Fleury of the Seattle Seahawks reacts after practice at Virginia Mason Athletic Center on July 25, 2026 in Renton, Washington. (Photo by Jack Compton/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Seattle Seahawks have established a clear identity under Mike Macdonald. The next step is determining how that identity continues to evolve as Seattle enters another season with a roster increasingly suited to what Macdonald wants to accomplish. That was the focus of my latest episode of The Hawks Eye, where I was joined by Griffin Sturgeon ( aka cmikesspinmove ) of the Seattle Overload Podcast . Rather than focusing on individual camp performances or projecting the depth chart, our conversation centered on a larger question: How can Seattle become more difficult to prepare for schematically on both sides of the football? Creating conflict on defense For me, the next stage of the defense begins with multiplicity. That does not necessarily mean expanding the playbook with an overwhelming number of new calls. The greater advantage is having personnel capable of presenting several different structures without substituting. Seattle could potentially show a traditional nickel alignment before shifting into a five-man surface, presenting pressure from multiple locations and ultimately rushing four. The same personnel could provide answers in big nickel, dime or heavier fronts depending on the opponent and situation. That is where players with positional versatility become particularly valuable. Nick Emmanwori is an intriguing example. His combination of size and athleticism potentially gives Macdonald the ability to deploy him as more than a box player. There are opportunities to use him at nickel, as an overhang defender, drop him deep or even as a true edge defender based on specific matchup assignments. The more responsibilities players can legitimately handle, the less information Seattle has to provide an offense before the snap. Griffin and I also spent considerable time discussing the difference between bringing pressure and presenting pressure. Macdonald can threaten the line of scrimmage with linebackers and defensive backs, forcing the quarterback and offensive line to identify potential rushers and adjust protection. Seattle can then drop defenders into coverage and rush four from a completely different combination. The pressure does not necessarily have to arrive to affect the play; the presentation itself can influence protection rules, create favorable matchups and force the quarterback to process additional information. Creating conflict on offense Seattle can attempt to create similar conflict offensively under new offensive coordinator Brian Fleury. Fleury’s background naturally creates interest in what Seattle might incorporate from the Kyle Shanahan offensive tree. I do not view that as just copying concepts from the San Francisco 49ers. The more important element is understanding the principles that have made those offenses consistently challenging to defend. Condensed formations, purposeful motion, drop back pass concepts, personnel versatility and marrying the run game with play action can force defenses to defend several possibilities from an almost identical initial picture. Motion, in particular, can accomplish much more than creating movement before the snap. It can help identify coverage, alter formation strength, manipulate leverage and force defenders to communicate. It can also provide Sam Darnold with information before he begins working through his post-snap progression. Through training camp there has been a lot of pre-snap motion in Fleury’s play calls, particularly involving his tight ends. The same personnel grouping, formation and motion can potentially lead to outside zone, a complementary run concept, play action, a keeper, screen or explosive downfield opportunity. That is the offensive version of what Macdonald is attempting to accomplish defensively: make the opponent process more information while revealing as little as possible. Ultimately, Seattle’s next evolution may be about finding more ways to operate from the same personnel and presentations. Griffin and I explored these ideas in much greater detail on “Seattle’s Next Evolution: Macdonald’s Defense & Fleury’s Offense,” including potential defensive packages, pressure structures, personnel chess pieces, and the concepts Fleury could bring to Seattle’s offense. The full conversation is available now on The Hawks Eye for anyone interested in examining where the Seahawks could go next from a coaching and schematic perspective. Video

title: Seahawks Football 101: What are the different kind of cornerbacks?
summary: Cornerbacks. A position that, after quarterback, is arguably the hardest position in football to play. Between covering receivers, anticipate where the quarterback is going to throw, assist with run stopping, it is no wonder that claim is made. There are more there more than one flavor of cornerback on a team, and each has their […]
full_text: Cornerbacks. A position that, after quarterback, is arguably the hardest position in football to play. Between covering receivers, anticipate where the quarterback is going to throw, assist with run stopping, it is no wonder that claim is made. There are more there more than one flavor of cornerback on a team, and each has their own duties. In this continuation of Football 101, we will be diving into the three flavors of cornerbacks, and Seattle Seahawks xamples from both the past and present to have a visual of those particular flavors. Time to dive-on-in! Outside Corner: Richard Sherman/Josh Jobe If you think of cornerbacks, your first thought that comes to mind is likely the outside corner. They line up generally near the boundaries and across from the X-receivers and Z-receivers line up and cover them. Think of Richard Sherman and Josh Jobe. They generally rely on their speed, height, and and length to cover the opposing receiver on deep routes to either breakup the pass or snag the interception. They are generally between 6’0” to 6’2” and 185 to 200 lbs. On this day in 2014: The #Seahawks beat the #49ers in the NFC Championship Game which led to Richard Sherman giving us one of the best postgame interviews ever. Six years later, Sherman is back in the NFC Championship Game as a member of the #49ers . pic.twitter.com/hcbZPCgdzY — Ari Meirov (@MySportsUpdate) January 19, 2020 Nickel Cornerback: Devon Witherspoon/Walter Thurmond The nickel cornerback is one who replaces either a linebacker or defensive lineman and their goal is to cover the slot receiver, covering the middle of the field along with the safeties. They can also be utilized in blitz packages to assist in the pass rush. Super Bowl champions Devon Witherspoon and Walter Thurmond III are examples of nickel cornerbacks. They are generally around 5’9” to 6’0” and 180 to 190 lbs. 97 YARD PICK SIX FOR DEVON WITHERSPOON 🤯😱 @Seahawks extend their lead!! (via @NFL ) pic.twitter.com/FhyNUfoqFN — FOX Sports: NFL (@NFLonFOX) October 3, 2023 Apex/Big Cornerback: Nick Emmanwori/Jordan Babineaux The big cornerback, or as Sumer Sports dubs it the Apex position, is where a larger cornerback or safety replaces the traditional nickel cornerback or linebacker to assist in covering Y-receivers and tight ends. They can also still help in blitz packages to assist in the pass rush. Think of Jordan Babineaux from back in the Mike Holmgren years. Mike Macdonald expanded this position with Nick Emmanwori, thus creating the apex position variant of the big nickel, and moving him to outside cornerback, outside linebacker, defensive end, and edge to help disguise the defensive scheme. They are generally between 6’0” to 6’2” and 200 to 220 lbs. Nick Emmanwori flies around like a missile every week: 🔹 4 PBUs 🔹 0.5 sacks 🔹 5 tackles One of the most impactful rookies in the NFL pic.twitter.com/CURxSDPbGP — NFL Draft Files (@NFL_DF) November 10, 2025 Each cornerback variant has their role to play, and the Seahawks have a long history of impactful cornerbacks. Some like Witherspoon and Emmanwori can assist in multiple cornerback positions. Let me know, though, who is your favorite cornerback in Seahawks history? Who is on your Mt Rushmore of Seahawks Cornerbacks? What variant of cornerback is your favorite to watch? Post in the comments, and let’s have a discussion! Join the conversation! title: 49ers News: Congratulations to Hall-of-Famer Roger Craig
summary: Roger Craig’s path from kickball to Hall of Fame, with a lifelong teammate along for the ride (paywall) “Bill Walsh saw no reason to wait. Never mind that players were still in their tuxedo jackets on the night they received their Super Bowl rings after winning it all in 1984. The San Francisco 49ers coach […]
full_text: PALO ALTO, CA - JANUARY 20: Roger Craig #33 of the San Francisco 49ers carries the ball against the Miami Dolphins in Super Bowl XIX on January 20, 1985 at Stanford Stadium in Palo Alto, California. The 49ers won the Super Bowl 38-16. (Photo by Focus on Sport/Getty Images) | Getty Images Roger Craig’s path from kickball to Hall of Fame, with a lifelong teammate along for the ride (paywall) “Bill Walsh saw no reason to wait. Never mind that players were still in their tuxedo jackets on the night they received their Super Bowl rings after winning it all in 1984. The San Francisco 49ers coach pulled Roger Craig aside during the gala and looked him in the eyes. “Roger, we’re going to need 1,000 yards from you next season,” the running back remembered him saying. This inspired Craig but also befuddled him. He was coming off a year in which he amassed 600-plus yards as a runner and as a receiver. “I was fired up. I knew I couldn’t let him down,” Craig once said. “But then I started to wonder if he meant he needed 1,000 yards rushing or receiving. “I wanted to cover my ass, so I figured I better shoot for both.” Craig did as instructed, delivering the first 1,000-1,000 season in NFL history in 1985, a milestone matched only by Marshall Faulk (1999) and Christian McCaffrey (2019). That distinction goes a long way toward explaining why Craig will be enshrined in the Pro Football Hall of Fame on Saturday.” Williams will stand onstage with his best friend when Craig’s bust is unveiled. What will he feel in that moment? Williams said he didn’t know. Then he became emotional. “You can’t write the script,” he said. “Facts get stranger than fiction. Somebody lives half a block from you, and you start out down by the docks trying to catch catfish. Then you both go on this long journey in life.” Montana wasn’t the first future Hall of Fame player who wondered what was up with Craig and Williams. In 1983, at the Hula Bowl in Honolulu, Pittsburgh quarterback Dan Marino and SMU running back Eric Dickerson were fascinated by the inseparable Nebraska teammates. “They couldn’t get their heads around the fact that we were two Black guys from Iowa,” Williams said. “Marino was like, ‘Man that sounds so boring. What did you all do?’ Then I started going down the list and they got jealous.” They rode horses. Fished. Roller-skated. Blasted the Jackson Five. They hid Roger in the trunk on trips to the drive-in, saving the admission money for candy. ….In the offseasons, Craig worked out five days a week, starting at 6:30 a.m., beginning four weeks after the 49ers’ season ended. Track work. Weight room. Three days of hill work. Craig’s trainer, Raymond Farris, calls Craig “Mr. Football” due to his devotion. Craig would be so eager to start their early morning sessions that Farris would often need to remind him: “Roger, you have to stretch.” Jerry Rice is synonymous with “The Hill,” but he learned how to conquer it from Craig, a 1983 second-round pick who arrived two years before Rice was drafted. “I’ll never forget the first day Jerry showed up and he couldn’t do it,” Farris said. “He hurt so badly afterward that he didn’t come back for the rest of that offseason.”…..“Roger was the only guy who loved training camp and looked forward to it,” wide receiver Mike Wilson said. “I dreaded going to Rocklin. I would be like, ‘Roger, really? You’ve got to be kidding me, man.’” How Romello Height’s winding path to the 49ers made him no ordinary rookie (paywall) I would go up against some good really good players at Auburn — I was on the scout team — and I got scout team player of the year my freshman year. So that’s honestly when I realized, ‘Man, I got it. All I gotta do is just continue to stack the days, work hard and my time will come.’ ” He transferred to USC, where … well, let’s not criticize a young man too much for having fun, but Height began having trouble showing up on time for classes and team meetings. “I was just all over the place, and I knew I had to change and mature in so many ways,” Height said. He often thought of his dad, Ronnie, the ex-Marine. “If he could have gotten his hands on me around that time, he probably would’ve strangled me,” Height said. “I got caught up in a lot of stuff, and that wasn’t how I was raised. I had to find myself, and once I did, man, I was on the right road.” The next stop was Georgia Tech, close to home in Dublin, Ga. Height loved it there. “They told me as soon as I came in the building, like, ‘Mello, just get off of the ball and play how you want. Go get the quarterback or whoever has the ball,’ ” Height said. “They fit the scheme around me.” He would have stayed at Georgia Tech, but like a far-off dinner bell, the pull of NIL was drool-inducing. So, Height became a Texas Tech Red Raider, and the school got its money’s worth — a player who was the product of his father and his previous three stops. “Four schools is a lot, and I was just trying to find myself,” Height said. “All those stops came with maturing. And by the time I got to Texas Tech, I was a totally different person. “I was taking care of my body. I was living in the building. I was creating bonds with my teammates. I was finally the best version of myself.” ….. “I’ve never seen a (rookie) come in and get the scheme as quickly and seamlessly as he has,” Bosa told KNBR radio. “Even when vets come in who haven’t played in this scheme. He’s gotten it even quicker than I did. “He’s super explosive. He’s got a bag of tricks in pass rush that you could tell he’s been coached well. He’s a little older for a rookie, so that might be part of it, but I think he’s going to contribute pretty quick.” Height credits the staff at Texas Tech with stuffing his bag full of pass-rush moves, especially the chop. During training camp, he has been focused on making blockers pay for being on their heels waiting for a speed rush. “I’ve been just trying to throw power in my tool bag,” he said. “That makes tackles more vulnerable to inside moves, more vulnerable to the speed that I’m gonna use because they’re just gonna sit on speed if I’m just showing continuous speed.” 49ers DC Raheem Morris explains the term ‘fever backer’ in his defense “Morris also referenced the term “spinner,” which is something Pete Carroll did with the Seahawks when they had a bunch of pass rushers early in the LOB days. Their “spinner” was mainly Bruce Irvin. To me, that’s who I envision the 49ers think Romello Height will be. More recently, that was Jalon Walker for the Falcons last season. A spinner is an edge rusher in name, but the defensive lineman who will move around the line of scrimmage. The uber-athlete who will line up everywhere, whether it’s over the left guard, right tackle, or blitzing from the stacked linebacker spot…..The 49ers won’t be nearly as static as they’ve been if they are anything like the Falcons from a season ago. There are several benefits to late movement or crowding the line of scrimmage with different body types. You can manipulate protections, create confusion, and get the offensive line to set or slide the wrong way. It’s a way to create free runners. It also gives the defense a way to tee off on the running back in 1-on-1 situations. Occasionally, we’ll see Height drop into coverage, but if his usage is anything like Walker’s last season, he’ll be one of the key pieces to the 49ers’ defense in 2026.” Five bright spots from 49ers training camp inspire optimism amid glut of injuries (paywall) “Rookies tend to err on the quieter side. Defensive tackle Gracen Halton has been in pads only for the past couple of days, returning from a knee bone bruise that sidelined him for five practices. Loud and proud is more his style. The 49ers drafted Halton, listed at 6-foot-2 and 293 pounds, in the fourth round out of Oklahoma. He started his college career as a defensive end and boasts noticeable explosiveness off the snap for an interior lineman. Starting center Jake Brendel, among others, saw as much…

His worst game that season was against the Niners on the road in Week 11. The Cardinals released Smith at the end of the 2023 training camp. He ended up bouncing around from there. title: Day 8 of 49ers Training Camp News & Notes: Kyle Shanahan is close to a full-time return
summary: The major story from training camp for the San Francisco 49ers has been injuries. Still, while the injuries don’t seem season-altering and are more bumps and bruises, the 49ers are using caution; the best news is that 49ers head coach Kyle Shanahan is inching closer to a return. Following his major car accident, the coach […]
full_text: The major story from training camp for the San Francisco 49ers has been injuries. Still, while the injuries don’t seem season-altering and are more bumps and bruises, the 49ers are using caution; the best news is that 49ers head coach Kyle Shanahan is inching closer to a return. Following his major car accident, the coach has been spotted out on the field for longer periods of time and is getting closer to the action on the field. Yes, football is played by football players, but nobody is more important to the 49ers than Shanahan. Here are some news and notes from day eight of 49ers training camp: The left guard competition has taken a turn Early on in training camp, Connor Colby was running with the first-team offense since he has experience in the system. It did seem as if the 49ers were giving the second-year guard the first crack at the competition. Offensive line coach Chris Foerster called Colby “the incumbent.” He did state that veteran Robert Jones would also get a shot with the ones. Fast forward to day eight, and Jones has run with the starting offense two straight practices. ESPN ’s Nick Wagoner doesn’t know if the long-term answer at left guard is on the roster. “Another day with the 1s at LG for Robert Jones, who is going to get a good look there, it seems. Connor Colby ran with the 2s and 3s again, including on the right side. And Pleasants got some more work at guard, too. My early read: The Niners are going to have to keep looking for the best option for LG. Not sure that person is on the roster, though the concussion for Carver Willis is unfortunate because he might have been able to force his way into the conversation.” Jack Jones isn’t going away The 49ers signed Jones this offseason in an effort to push third-year cornerback Renardo Green. The plan seems to be working, with Raheem Morris praising Green as the secondary as a whole has earned rave reviews during training camp. While I expect Green to start opposite Deommodore Lenoir, Jones is keeping himself in the conversation with what seems to be a highlight play each day of camp. Wagoner shares the same sentiment. “CB Jack Jones finds a way to make a play in practice nearly every day and did so again today. He jumped in front of a crosser from Mac Jones for Jordan Watkins for an interception. It wasn’t an easy one, either, as Jones tapped it to himself with his right hand then hauled it in.” The depth at cornerback has never been better. Demarcus Robinson has gone from bubble player to near lock for the roster With Ricky Pearsall done for the season, the 49ers pivoted to bringing back Deebo Samuel. Christian Kirk is also banged up. Demarcus Robinson has gone from a luxury roster spot to a necessity. Mike Evans and De’Zhaun Stribling figure to dominate two-receiver sets, with Samuel being used all over the field in different situations, but Robinson is a veteran who has Shanahan’s trust. Generally, if you don’t play special teams as a backup, you won’t make the roster, but Robinson is the exception. The six receivers the 49ers will likely keep are Evans, Stribling, Kirk, Samuel, Robinson, and Jacob Cowing. Jordan Watkins is on the outside looking in with no real development or special teams spot. Cowing has experience fielding punts in the NFL.
author: Jason Aponte

title: Are you drafting 49ers RB Christian McCaffrey in fantasy football?
summary: 2025 was a banner season for Christian McCaffrey in fantasy football land. The San Francisco 49ers offense was down many pieces, but McCaffrey was the constant and a force. Fantasy football managers were rewarded for their gamble with the overall RB1. Plain and simple, if you drafted McCaffrey, you probably won your league. But what […]
full_text: 2025 was a banner season for Christian McCaffrey in fantasy football land. The San Francisco 49ers offense was down many pieces, but McCaffrey was the constant and a force. Fantasy football managers were rewarded for their gamble with the overall RB1. Plain and simple, if you drafted McCaffrey, you probably won your league. But what about 2026? Following a season with 450 touches, including the postseason, the running back is entering his year 30 season. There is no doubt of McCaffrey’s ability on the field, but the concern is a potential injury. I spoke with former NFL Network and CBS Sports fantasy football analyst Michael Fabiano about drafting McCaffrey and his thought process entering last year’s draft about CMC. The Sports Illustrated analyst admits he faded McCaffrey last season, which was a mistake, and only has Bijan Robinson and Jahmyr Gibbs ahead of McCaffrey in 2026, but is proceeding with caution. “ I was wrong about him last year. I was right about Barkley, I was right about Jaxon Smith-Njigba, I was right about Drake Maye. CMC was my biggest whiff. Because I didn’t say not to draft him, I just said I don’t wanna draft him in the first round, and if you didn’t draft him in the first round, you weren’t getting him. The durability issues were huge for me. The previous year he had only played four games, and he averaged, like, 12 points per game in those games, and you started to wonder i- if there were gonna be, you know, suddenly some kinks in the armor. And then last year he went nuts. On a Niners team that had all kinds of injuries, he was the one durable dude, right? So, I mean, go figure. The fantasy football gods are laughing at us. But I think the same concerns are very, very realistic right now, and maybe even more so. He had 450 touches last year, 450 between the regular season and playoffs. That is a ton of work for a guy who’s 30. And now you’re playing in an offense that is like a mash unit.“ Personally, I can never bring myself to draft McCaffrey. You can’t win your league in the first round, but you sure can lose it, and I never can risk my first-round pick. If you did last season, man, you were rewarded. I’m not sure I will draft him if available in the first round, but you know what they say: No risk it, no biscuit. What are your thoughts on McCaffrey in fantasy football this season? Will you be drafting him? Let us know in the comments! For a longer discussion featuring Fabiano, check out the video below:

title: 49ers DC Raheem Morris explains the term ‘fever backer’ in his defense
summary: By now, you’re well aware that the San Francisco 49ers are operating a new scheme under Raheem Morris. It seems like there’s a daily question for one of the offensive players or staff about the difference in Morris’s defense. On Thursday, Morris admitted that he’s “making up a lot of terms” since he’s been with […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - MAY 28: Romello Height #94 of the San Francisco 49ers works out during a team OTA practice at SAP Performance Facility on May 28, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images) | Getty Images By now, you’re well aware that the San Francisco 49ers are operating a new scheme under Raheem Morris. It seems like there’s a daily question for one of the offensive players or staff about the difference in Morris’s defense. On Thursday, Morris admitted that he’s “making up a lot of terms” since he’s been with the 49ers. One of those terms is “fever backer.” Here’s what that position is, according to Morris: Obviously, you know what traditional backers look like. Stand-up guys that can move around. Those fever backers are kind of those guys that bring you subtle changes, subtle different things. They can do different things. They can play star for you. They can play outside edge and play sort of a big nickel. They can get at the line of scrimmage. They can use their hands, do a couple different things. We’ve got a couple different terms for what those styles look like and what they feel like in order to get guys lined up, put them on paper. Nick Martin. Jaden Dugger. Larry Worth. Those are the three players to keep an eye on in these roles. Those are the players who can rush the passer, play underneath coverage, and set the edge in the running game. Morris also referenced the term “spinner,” which is something Pete Carroll did with the Seahawks when they had a bunch of pass rushers early in the LOB days. Their “spinner” was mainly Bruce Irvin. To me, that’s who I envision the 49ers think Romello Height will be. More recently, that was Jalon Walker for the Falcons last season. A spinner is an edge rusher in name, but the defensive lineman who will move around the line of scrimmage. The uber-athlete who will line up everywhere, whether it’s over the left guard, right tackle, or blitzing from the stacked linebacker spot. Morris mentioned spinner a few times on Thursday, including when talking about Height: Obviously, on tape you saw the designated pass rusher role that you can feel that we lost from the team from the year before. So, he can come in and feel some of those things. Then there was some further thoughts, some things that we could possibly do with him, whether it be fever backer, whether it be spinner, whatever it is, being able to get him out of different roles. Then you’ve got to meet the young man to find out what his learning capacity is. Can he handle those things from a down-in, down-out basis? And he’s done a really nice job of handling those things throughout the course of training camp. That’s all you really can say. The 49ers won’t be nearly as static as they’ve been if they are anything like the Falcons from a season ago. There are several benefits to late movement or crowding the line of scrimmage with different body types. You can manipulate protections, create confusion, and get the offensive line to set or slide the wrong way. It’s a way to create free runners. It also gives the defense a way to tee off on the running back in 1-on-1 situations. Occasionally, we’ll see Height drop into coverage, but if his usage is anything like Walker’s last season, he’ll be one of the key pieces to the 49ers’ defense in 2026.
author: Kyle Posey

title: Mac Jones has a nickname for 49ers’ rookie De’Zhaun Stribling
summary: The San Francisco 49ers got rookie De’Zhaun Stribling back at practice. The receiver has been out as the team managed Stribling’s hamstring tightness a week ago. Backup quarterback Mac Jones was asked what Stribling brings to the table that wasn’t in the receiver room last year. From there, Jones said what he calls Stribling: Definitely. […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - JULY 27: De'Zhaun Stribling #15 of the San Francisco 49ers works out during training camp practice at SAP Performance Facility on July 27, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers got rookie De’Zhaun Stribling back at practice. The receiver has been out as the team managed Stribling’s hamstring tightness a week ago. Backup quarterback Mac Jones was asked what Stribling brings to the table that wasn’t in the receiver room last year. From there, Jones said what he calls Stribling: Definitely. Yeah, I call him the Flyin’ Hawaiian because he’s so fast. But he definitely is fast, but some guys, they can be really quick, but they’re not as strong, so he has both. I don’t have a comp for him yet, but I think he’ll be a really good player. The 49ers will need Stribling to live up to his draft status after the Ricky Pearsall news . We’re hearing about players like Demarcus Robinson and Junior Bergen flash at the position. Things might be different this year for Robinson with a player like Mike Evans on the roster, but we’re also talking about a 10-year veteran and a 7th-round second-year pro. Jones has more to say about Stribling: “And I don’t know, just the way he got to the ball when it’s in the air was impressive. He has like a second gear when the ball’s in the air. Some guys are really fast, but when the ball goes up and your eyes go up, you slow down, but he doesn’t do that, so it’s pretty impressive. So, you want to have guys like that, and speed is good, but you want ball speed where the ball’s in the air that you don’t slow down. So he has that.” Jones also mentioned Evans and Jordan Watkins as players who can do that. Watkins will need to improve on his consistency catching the ball. Not only outright catching the ball, but also not letting it get into his shoulder pads. Keep an eye out for that during the preseason. Jones spoke about Watkins in-depth: “Yeah, I really like Jordan. He’s one of my good buddies on the team, and he’s always got a good attitude. He just goes out there and runs fast. With us, we’re very similar because we’re hard on ourselves. So, like, if he has a bad play, I always try to, like, go up to him and be like, ‘Hey, play the next play. It’s all good.’ Similar with me, if I have a bad play, I want him to do the same, and we kind of have that relationship. So, for him, it’s just playing that next play as best he can, and he’s done a better job of that this training camp, and he’s really fast and has a lot of talent and has played in a lot of big-time football in college, so, you know that he has what it takes to be really good.” Watkins is the kind of player who can raise the ceiling of the offense if he can string it all together. The athleticism is there. Now it’s about whether he can get used to the physicality of the NFL and everything that comes with the down-to-down duties of a receiver. Jones has noticed some of the younger wideouts stepping up and making plays. He name-dropped Bergen, specifically knowing what to do while playing fast. It’s one thing to run fast on a stopwatch. It’s another to play fast as you’re processing what the defense is doing. Bergen looks to slide into the role of Jacob Cowing, whose time is likely up after suffering a hip flexor. There are plenty of battles that will play out in August. Players like Malik Turner get another life with other players sitting out. Will they take advantage of their opportunities?
author: Kyle Posey

summary: 49ers sign former Dolphins starting guard; waive receiver“No surprise, as the 49ers made an official move to add a lineman. They signed Kion Smith. The corresponding move was to waive Colton Dowell. Smith started the first three games of the season for Miami last year at right guard. He was good for the first two […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - AUGUST 10: Kion Smith #71 Miami Dolphins works against Jonathan Ford #64 of the Chicago Bears during an NFL preseason football game between the Miami Dolphins and the Chicago Bears at Soldier Field on August 10, 2025, in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Kara Durrette/Getty Images) | Getty Images 49ers sign former Dolphins starting guard; waive receiver “No surprise, as the 49ers made an official move to add a lineman. They signed Kion Smith. The corresponding move was to waive Colton Dowell. Smith started the first three games of the season for Miami last year at right guard. He was good for the first two games, but struggled in the third game against the Bills, based on his blown block rate.” The Good and Not So Good from Day 8 of 49ers Camp: Brock Purdy is Raising his Game “Absolutely eviscerated the starting defense today while throwing to wide receivers named Malik Turner and KhaDarel Hodge. Technically, Purdy’s No. 1 receiver on the field is Deebo Samuel, but he can’t get open, so Purdy is forced to go through his progressions and fire tight-window throws to players who may or may not make the final roster. And despite all this, he threw two deep touchdown passes today and no interceptions. In fact, he has thrown just one interception in all of camp. He’s making good, quick decisions, and he’s playing with the most confidence I’ve ever seen from him. There’s no question that he’s having the best camp of his career. Unfortunately for him, his offensive line is shaky, his running game is non-existent and his receivers mostly are injured. The 49ers need to get him some help before he gets injured like last season.” 49ers’ Mac Jones, Raheem Morris share Week 3 training camp updates “’The layer king’ has some really intensive intensity, and I like that about him. It’s really fun for me when you get a chance to get some of those call-it periods and you get a chance to go in the back with the offense and you call your play and you get a chance to just hear him operate. You’re listening to him and you’re able to hear him operate and you’re able to hear him operate in a very pro manner. How he communicates with the coaches, how he’s very up front. Today he got fired up, which was cool, which was fun, which was competitive, and I love that. When he does those things, it just makes the team go. I watch that team go out there and basically have a fight for an hour and a half, and then hug at the end of practice and cheer for each other. It’s the weirdest thing ever. It’s awesome. It was a lot of fun with that guy. He’s awesome.” Brock Purdy impresses new 49ers DC Raheem Morris with layered throws in practice “Yes, Purdy hooked up on a couple of deep passes, but the best play was what one sideline observer immediately described as, “Good on good.” There was nothing wrong with the coverage of cornerback Deommodore Lenoir and Brown. But there was nothing that could be done to prevent a completion on a deep crossing route with Purdy’s perfect throw and Deebo Samuel’s contested catch.”

The deal makes him the highest-paid guard in the league. Skoronski officially signed the deal this afternoon: It is nice to see a homegrown guy get an extension. That is how […]

title: Will Titans WR Carnell Tate be the next rookie 1,000 yard receiver?
summary: The Tennessee Titans decided to spend their fourth overall selection in the 2026 NFL Draft by investing in franchise quarterback Cam Ward. They took former Ohio State wide receiver Carnell Tate with the pick. Tate is expected to immediately play a legitimate role in Brian Daboll’s offense in 2026. Tate was excellent at OTAs, catching […]
full_text: Jun 16, 2026; Nashville, TN, USA; Tennessee Titans wider receiver Carnell Tate (14) makes a catch during day 1 of mini-camp at Vanderbilt Health Football Center. Mandatory Credit: Steve Roberts-Imagn Images | Steve Roberts-Imagn Images The Tennessee Titans decided to spend their fourth overall selection in the 2026 NFL Draft by investing in franchise quarterback Cam Ward. They took former Ohio State wide receiver Carnell Tate with the pick . Tate is expected to immediately play a legitimate role in Brian Daboll’s offense in 2026. Tate was excellent at OTAs , catching three touchdowns at the first open practice. He continued to grow and develop at minicamp. We’re now officially underway at training camp, where Tate has taken advantage of additional opportunities to get better and develop chemistry with Ward. It wouldn’t be shocking if Tate was the primary read on most passing dropbacks . Of course there will be competition for targets though. The Titans signed Wan’Dale Robinson to a $70 million contract in free agency. Robinson knows Daboll’s offense. Mike Borgonzi also retained Calvin Ridley via a restructured contract. Chimere Dike and Elic Ayomanor are developing sophomores. Ayomanor and Ridley have been good at camp. The Titans are deeper at receiver than they’ve ever been, but Tate is still expected to be a focal point. Rookie wideouts have hit the ground running in recent years. There’s been a 1,000-yard rookie receiver every year in the NFL since 2019, starting with the Titans and A.J. Brown. We had Justin Jefferson in 2020, Ja’Marr Chase and Jaylen Waddle in 2021, Garrett Wilson and Chris Olave in 2022, Puka Nacua in 2023, Malik Nabers, Ladd McConkey, and Brian Thomas Jr. in 2024, and Tetairoa McMillan in 2025. Brock Bowers and Kyle Pitts also achieved it from the tight end position. Of all the rookie receivers in the NFL this season, Tate certainly possesses the best opportunity to produce 1,000 yards. He has Daboll as his offensive coordinator and a developing franchise quarterback in Ward. We’ll see how the Titans’ depth at receiver impacts Tate. He possesses every trait in the right environment to be this year’s 1,000 yard rookie wideout.

title: Is the Commanders secondary going through a changing of the guard?
summary: Commanders starters in the secondary appeared to be set after free agency and the NFL draft, with Trey Amos, Mike Sainristil, and Amik Robertson working in a rotation along with safeties Nick Cross, Will Harris, and Quan Martin. New coordinator Daronte Jones specifically mentioned both Sainristil and Martin as players he liked for their versatility […]
full_text: Commanders starters in the secondary appeared to be set after free agency and the NFL draft, with Trey Amos, Mike Sainristil, and Amik Robertson working in a rotation along with safeties Nick Cross, Will Harris, and Quan Martin. New coordinator Daronte Jones specifically mentioned both Sainristil and Martin as players he liked for their versatility in his introductory presser , and there were early predictions of a bounce-back season for both. Headed into the second week of training camp, the early picture has become a lot less clear. The addition of Rasul Douglas coincided with Trey Amos being placed on the active/physically unable to perform list and was written off as merely a depth/insurance signing by some. In contrast, Douglas has looked good in early work, holding his own versus the likes of Terry McLaurin and generating multiple turnovers, including a pick-six . Meanwhile, Sainristil’s transition to the new scheme has not been as smooth. He has had some nice pass breakups and coverage plays, but also a number of bad plays to start camp, including more than one dropped interception. He has also struggled to cover Washington’s second-string wide receivers. Jayden Daniels tried to throw a deep ball to Antonio Williams in double coverage, and Mike Sainristil dropped the interception. #Commanders — Josh Taylor (@JoshTaylorFB) August 7, 2026 I’m sorry, but Mike Sainristil hasn’t moved me at all this camp. Hopefully it picks up at the joint practice. — Josh Taylor (@JoshTaylorFB) August 7, 2026 Last year the yellow caution flag was raised watching Mike Sainristil, so far in camp that yellow is turning closer to red. He’s getting cooked on the daily. — DC Sports 💯 (@DCSportsInSD) August 7, 2026 It is still very early in camp, and there is plenty of time to develop in Jones’ scheme. At the moment, it appears to be Robertson and Douglas as the favorites to line up opposite Amos down the line. While the inside may be a better fit for Sainristil, with Jones’ supposed preference for three-safety looks, it is yet to be determined how much playing time Mike would see in the slot, but he needs to improve in practice to claim it. LOT of talk about #Commanders CB Mike Sainristil on the timeline. It's been tough recently, but CB is the ultimate confidence position. It comes and goes. He'll get his swagger back and, like Jayden Daniels, get back closer to his rookie form. Go get it done, 0. #RaiseHail pic.twitter.com/iOwhhLyLw6 — District Divided (@DistrictDivided) August 7, 2026 Speaking of the safeties, free agent addition Nick Cross has lived up to his hype so far, and he looks like a force. However, instead of Harris or Martin, so far it has been Jeremy Reaves given the first chance to start next to Cross in two-high safety looks. Given his lack of high-end athleticism, Reaves may seem like a questionable fit, but head coach Dan Quinn has praised his football IQ and communication skills, two things Jones covets in his defense. His communication skills are elite as a ball player is, as a teammate on the field and off,” Quinn said at his Wednesday presser . “So much of what we’re doing goes through out communication hub at linebacker and safety, so seeing him and Frankie (Luvu) and others…he’s an initiator of so many good things that we talk through. He sets incredible standards for effort and speed. While Harris may prove to be the more natural fit, Reaves is getting a well-deserved chance to prove he belongs. Martin was projected to bounce back with a move to a slot/hybrid role in Jones’ scheme but so far has failed to distinguish himself. In his place, third-year safety Tyler Owens is getting more looks. At yesterday's practice, Tyler Owens lined up as an off ball LB, BIGN/Slot, ILB, & FS in different looks. Daronte Jones is giving these dudes opportunities. No more excuses. #RaiseHail #Commanders — Deuce_Redzone (@redzoneinthelab) August 5, 2026 Pains me to say this but after every camp day I’ve attended I get more and more convinced that Quan Martin is a prime cut candidate — Bleeding Burgundy & Gold (@BleedinBnG) August 7, 2026 The narrative that some of these players may be cut after less than two weeks of camp work is extreme to say the least, but it does demonstrate the early impressions of their performance from a fan’s view at training camp. There is still plenty of time to claim more playing time, but both Martin and Sainristil have something to prove next week in the Commanders’ joint practice session with Miami. Both players may be struggling some as they are asked to play in a new role within a different scheme. But, for Sainristil in particular, his success is tied to finding the right fit. So far, the Washington Commanders have yet to find it. Always enjoy catching up with @FelixDTrammell on @DougMcCrayNFL and my show! We covered a lot of ground, but this was my favorite clip. (Photo by Fred Kfoury III/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Training camp rolls on and the Washington Commanders continue to tweak their roster for competition, and also to deal with injuries and retirements. Washington released OL Tyler Cooper yesterday to open a roster spot for WR Stefon Diggs, and they have now reportedly added another veteran offensive lineman to the roster. Max Scharping was a second-round pick by the Houston Texans in 2019. He started 33 regular season and two playoff games in Houston before getting released during the final roster cutdowns in his fourth season. Scharping was claimed off waivers by the Cincinnati Bengals, but only played 43 snaps on offense for them over two seasons. He did start three games in the playoffs in his first year with the Bengals. Scharping then took a mini-tour of the NFC East with brief stints in Philadelphia and Washington in 2024. He ended up going back to the AFC North, signing with the Pittsburgh Steelers, but he only appeared in two games over two seasons. Scharping tore his ACL in September last year. The Commanders offensive line has been dealing with a calf injury to projected starting center Nick Allegretti that has forced them to work other players at the position and sign another player to allow camp reps to continue on schedule. The right guard position is locked down by Sam Cosmi, while left guard is a repeat of last year’s battle between Brandon Coleman and Chris Paul. The interior depth can always be improved, but Scharping looks like a camp body, with a possibility to make the practice squad eventually. title: How Stefon Diggs made a great first impression on Washington Commanders
summary: Stefon Diggs finished his first practice with the Commanders, got in some extra work with quarterback Jayden Daniels and then headed to his formal introductory press conference.   The veteran receiver quickly noted that the media tent was a sauna, the microphones used to ask questions were too low and that bugs circling the dais […]
full_text: Stefon Diggs finished his first practice with the Commanders, got in some extra work with quarterback Jayden Daniels and then headed to his formal introductory press conference. The veteran receiver quickly noted that the media tent was a sauna, the microphones used to ask questions were too low and that bugs circling the dais wouldn’t leave him alone. None of that deterred him from saying all the right things. The DMV native and University of Maryland product won the press conference and surely the hearts and minds of Commanders fans listening in, exuding joy while reveling in the great fortune of playing for his hometown team. Diggs spent months on the open market, well after most unrestricted free agents had signed, waiting for just the right opportunity. He found it in Washington, with a team needing his expertise to reclaim 2024 glory after a down season. Diggs was glad he waited for just the right opportunity in just the right place. Best of Stef Diggs first practice in Ashburn pic.twitter.com/GoCKvbiUEZ — JP Finlay (@JPFinlayNBCS) August 7, 2026 “We had an idea that we wanted to slow-play it and so whatever made the most sense at this stage of my career,” Diggs said in his Friday press conference. “Everybody knows I want to win and I want to hold a trophy up. What better place to do it than back home? I have to work every day in order to do that but, here I am, putting one foot in front of the other. “I take it one day at a time and try to treat things organically. Gratitude eliminates entitlement. I come in grateful and happy to be here.” That was clear during the 13 minutes, 46 seconds spent at the podium, even with the bugs and DMV humidity he didn’t miss from his younger days. He called Daniels a superstar. Diggs said Terry McLaurin is a like mind who plays with his level of passion. He said rookie Antonio Williams “can hoop,” even though young players get mentioned by number and not name at this early stage. Head coach Dan Quinn said he played against Diggs a ton and had seen the quality game film, but he learned this week about Diggs’ willingness to lead and assist and set high standards. That was clear on Day 1, with extra time spent with Daniels, McLaurin and so many of the young Commanders players on both sides of the ball. The 32-year-old takes pride in doing all that, hoping to elevate the play of those around him. “I always try to push the guys around me to be the best version of themselves,” Diggs said. “We’re building that already. It’s Day 1, but we had a lot of conversations, more than I thought we would have, with guys coming up to me. I’ve been around for a while and I’m trying to give them everything I’ve got. “…I want to keep that good energy going and be a beacon of light and bring a positive energy and a dog mindset. I want to show more than I tell. I talk to y’all a lot but, out there, it’s all ball.” Where he’s playing football makes this experience already hits different. That was clear when reporters started bringing up his youth football days played around his native Gaithersburg, MD. Diggs was born and raised in the DMV. He went to college here and now makes a return home as a professional entering his 12 th NFL season . “I got chills just now…I can’t write a better story,” Diggs said. “At this point in my career, with what I want to do, being able to be healthy, coming off an ACL and having success and then coming to your hometown team and wanting to shine for them – I want to put on for my city. I wanted to do that when I was away, and I want to do that when I’m home. “It definitely means a lot to me. Pulling your heartstrings a little bit, but I know I’ve got a city behind me. I’ve got a support system here and I know I have a lot of love here. I want to make people proud. The best way you can do that is to go far. I’m not going to say where – I don’t want to jinx it or nothing – but I want to go far and be consistent and be a puzzle piece that affects this team in a positive way.” Stefon Diggs gets emotional when asked what a younger him would have thought about playing for the hometown team in Burgundy and Gold pic.twitter.com/kN0zZi9T7H — COMMANDERS FOOTBALL (@HogsHaven) August 7, 2026 Diggs promises not to force it. He’ll immerse himself into the Commanders culture slowly and without entitlement. After months without a team, Diggs is clearly intrigued by a new opportunity with great promise. “I’ve been around the game for a long time,” Diggs said. “I have been productive. I know my way around the field a little bit, so I come with some experience. With leadership, I know everyone is led differently. I’m new here, so I’m just trying to earn my keep and earn the respect of my teammates and coaches. Most importantly, right now, is to learn the playbook. I’m a little late in the game, but I’m going to handle it the right way, life a professional. I’m just excited to be at work.”

title: Commanders activate Trey Amos off physically unable to perform list
summary: Trey Amos is back. And he isn’t the only Commander now cleared to practice. The second-year cornerback was cleared for practice and taken off the active/physically unable to perform list, the team announced on Friday morning. There was no corresponding move because Amos already counted against the Washington’s roster. Washington also activated edge rusher Dorance […]
full_text: Trey Amos is back. And he isn’t the only Commander now cleared to practice. The second-year cornerback was cleared for practice and taken off the active/physically unable to perform list, the team announced on Friday morning. There was no corresponding move because Amos already counted against the Washington’s roster. Washington also activated edge rusher Dorance Armstrong (knee) off active/PUP and brought punter Tress Way (pectoral) off the non-football injury list. Again, no corresponding move was required as both players already counted towards the offseason roster limit. Head coach Dan Quinn said Armstrong will be brought along slowly , in walk throughs and lighter activity, as they build him up. Dan Quinn says Dorance Armstrong will be doing individual work as he returns to practice for the first time since tearing his ACL last October. pic.twitter.com/UgyIoXQBNz — COMMANDERS FOOTBALL (@HogsHaven) August 7, 2026 Washington placed Amos on active/PUP on July 25, after the initial wave of Commanders reported to training camp. While the 2025 second-round draft pick has not practiced or played with the team since suffering a fractured fibula on Nov. 9, 2024, in a Week 10 loss to the Detroit Lions , head coach Dan Quinn said he had been sidelined while dealing with soft tissue soreness. Quinn also said that Amos and Way would be reassessed on Thursday by the team’s medical staff. Those evaluations obviously went well, as they passed a physical and will return to practice with the team. Amos is expected to be the top Commanders cornerback, a title earned with a strong start to his rookie campaign. Washington fortified its cornerback corps by signing veterans Rasul Douglas and Amik Robertson, who was back in action Friday after missing Wednesday’s practice for undisclosed reasons. Armstrong should be a rotational piece off the edge but will provide quality depth at that spot. While the Amos and Way returns were somewhat expected, the Armstrong news was a pleasant surprise. Defensive lineman Deatrich Wise (quadriceps) remains on active/PUP list.

title: Washington Commanders formally announce Stefon Diggs signing
summary: It’s now official. Stefon Diggs is a member of the Washington Commanders. The veteran receiver passed his physical and then signed his one-year contract. Washington formally announced the acquisition on Friday morning before the start of training camp practice. This formally secures Diggs’ services following a Wednesday pact that will pay up to $12 million […]
full_text: It’s now official. Stefon Diggs is a member of the Washington Commanders. The veteran receiver passed his physical and then signed his one-year contract. Washington formally announced the acquisition on Friday morning before the start of training camp practice. DIGGS (back) IN DC pic.twitter.com/stUjgxQyvg — Washington Commanders (@Commanders) August 7, 2026 This formally secures Diggs’ services following a Wednesday pact that will pay up to $12 million for the 2026 season . He arrived at the Commanders training complex on Thursday, an off day on the camp calendar, took his physical and met many in the organization. Now he has signed his contract. The Commanders released guard Tyler Cooper for the corresponding roster move. Diggs is expected to practice with the Commanders for the first time on Friday morning and hold a press conference after that. Diggs hit unrestricted free agency in March, when the New England Patriots released him after one season for financial reasons. He was excellent for them in 2025, with 85 catches for 1,013 receiving yards on just 105 targets. The veteran receiver will offer an instant upgrade to his position group and the Commanders offense overall, as an efficient and steady productive option for quarterback Jayden Daniels. He’s the best option opposite Terry McLaurin the Commanders have featured since drafting Daniels back in 2024. Diggs will need a ramp-up period in practice, but he has plenty of time to learn coordinator David Blough’s new offense and to build a rapport with Daniels. It will be interesting to see how quickly Diggs fits in with the Commanders entering his 10th NFL season, following an offseason spent training in full health. This story will be updated with Diggs’ jersey number when available.

full_text: LANDOVER, MARYLAND - NOVEMBER 02: Jayden Daniels #5 of the Washington Commanders warms up prior to the game against the Seattle Seahawks at Northwest Stadium on November 02, 2025 in Landover, Maryland. (Photo by Greg Fiume/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Daily Slop – 7 August 2026 Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy! Commanders links Articles Last Man Standig (paywall) What the Stefon Diggs signing says about Adam Peters in Year 3 Washington’s latest move isn’t just about adding another accomplished receiver. It suggests the Commanders’ GM has refined his approach after seeing how uncertainty can carry real football costs. All-Pro receiver Terry McLaurin. Depending on your perspective, Peters won that negotiation. Washington eventually reached an agreement on terms that, while setting up the 30-year-old McLaurin with a lucrative payday, were largely favorable to the organization. But there was another cost to that victory. McLaurin remained away from the team beginning during the spring offseason program and continuing through training camp. Tension from the standoff was felt daily in the team facility and all around the Beltway. Valuable practice time with Daniels entering his second season was lost. Then, after finally returning, McLaurin suffered an injury that sidelined him for seven games. When paired with McLaurin, Diggs provides Daniels with another proven target capable of punishing defenses that focus extra attention on Washington’s No. 1 receiver. If McLaurin misses time again, the Commanders now have someone who can approximate the responsibilities of a top option rather than forcing an entire committee into roles they may not be suited for. Should Father Time finally decide to wrestle Diggs into submission, Washington can pivot to its other viable options. For more from Ben Standig, click here The Athletic (paywall) Commanders takeaways after 6 practices Trey Amos still hasn’t returned to the field after suffering a fractured fibula in early November, which leaves him little time to get back into football shape for the season once he’s medically cleared. Washington brought in veteran Rasul Douglas for additional help, and recently signed Fabian Moreau following Ahkello Witherspoon’s abrupt retirement. But given the Commanders’ defensive shortcomings in recent years, it’s fair to wonder if that’s enough. Quinn never publicly tabbed one player to wear the green dot; he repeatedly said it would depend on the defensive package on the field and who seemed most comfortable in the role. He also said it could be a linebacker or a defensive back. After a week of camp, the primary guy has been Frankie Luvu. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Commanders.com Hail Mail | Kaytron Allen is a bowling ball @A_Smith_FS: Will JCM operate as the “lead” back? Or will White see a 50/50 split? @FantasyTags: What do you think the running back split looks like this season if both JCM & Rachaad stay healthy? That’s an interesting question, and I think there are a few factors at play here. Jacory Croskey-Merritt has burst and the ability to make explosive plays; Rachaad White is a fun addition as a pass-catcher; Kaytron Allen is your physical battering ram that can pick up the tough yards; and Jeremy McNichols can do a little of all three. There’s also Jerome Ford and Robert Henry Jr., who have flashed, but you can only keep so many players on the roster. I think labeling any player as the lead back right now and giving them most of the carries would somewhat hamstring the position group’s potential, because all of these guys can help you in games. However, I also believe there is a chance for Croskey-Merritt to take a leading role if he keeps showing improvement. I think the Commanders have been pushing him to show that, and to his credit, he has done so over the past week. The Commanders don’t just hand jobs to people; rather, they make them earn it. Croskey-Merritt has so much potential, and if he keeps standing out, I could see a world where he is their lead back. For now, however, I think the running back room will operate as The Avengers rather than Superman and Friends. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Sports Illustrated Winners and Losers From the Commanders’ First Week of Training Camp Winner: Luke McCaffrey Luke McCaffrey came to Commanders camp with the idea that the WR2 role was wide open and available to the player who was willing to take it. And that is just what he has done: play like he is trying to take that role. Of course, his case is built on several productive practices rather than one isolated catch or touchdown, even though he has had a few of those as well. McCaffrey has used the first week of camp to earn greater leverage and a stronger claim to more consistent offensive opportunities this season. While Stefon Diggs being signed all but killed any chance he has at WR2, his argument for WR3 is strong. Loser: The Kicking Competition Jake Moody and Drew Stevens entered camp without meaningful separation after ending minicamp 6-for-6 on the last day and initially matched one another through perfect kicking sessions the first few days of camp. The two have had some misses of late, which has left the competition without either kicker building any amount of momentum or giving Washington a clearer answer in the process. The competition has failed to deliver to this point as it sits pretty much in the same place it began a week ago. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Riggo’s Rag Commanders’ Antonio Williams quietly struck gold with the Stefon Diggs signing [T]he tide turned last season with Diggs. He reportedly emerged as a strong leader and mentor last season on the New England Patriots, emerging as the model teammate and barely putting a foot wrong. If the same player shows up in Washington, Williams would be wise to hang on his every word. Williams has the talent. He now has two top-level performers in Diggs and Terry McLaurin to lean on for advice, counsel, and some extra nuances that can help take his game to another level. Learning behind Diggs could be a blessing in disguise for Williams. It means he won’t be forced into a role beyond his present-day capabilities in his first NFL season, and he’ll be able to develop with patience and grace under Washington’s coaching staff. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Commanders Roundtable Jayden Daniels has drawn consistent praise in training camp With a chance to quiet critics, Washington Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels may be doing exactly that ahead of the start of the preseason slate. Redzone reps were the theme of the Commanders’ first few practices of training camp with a chance to evaluate both sides of the ball, such as rookie linebacker Sonny Styles making his presence felt with plays against running back Jacory Croskey-Merritt at the goal line in consecutive days. While new edge rusher Odafe Oweh has been hard to ignore while rookie wide receiver Antonio Williams has drawn praise for being fluid in his route tree, Daniels has remained a constant among the early takeaways. In Monday’s first padded practice of training camp, Daniels flashed his zip and accuracy inside the 20 after finding Terry McLaurin among others in the back of the end zone. Day two provided more of the same as Daniels once again connected with McLaurin on a beautiful throw that sailed just over the shoulder of cornerback Mike Sainristil, a play that drew praise. title: From ball boy to HOFer, inside Larry Fitzgerald's unique path
summary: After firing him, the Vikings rehired Fitzgerald as a ball boy and assigned him to the receivers, a move that shaped his career.
full_text:
A WEEK INTO the Minnesota Vikings ' 1999 training camp, the person in charge of checking media parking passes was fired. He had broken curfew, and then-coach Dennis Green wasn't having it.

 Neither was the young man's father. After all, Larry Fitzgerald Sr.'s relationship with Green was one of the reasons Larry Jr. got the gig.

 A week later, Green rehired Fitzgerald, but instead of parking lot attendant, Fitzgerald became the ball boy for the wide receivers. That episode played a significant role in the trajectory of Fitzgerald's career, which culminates Saturday when he's enshrined into the Pro Football Hall of Fame.

 "That's when," said Larry's brother, Marcus, "the true story of Larry Fitzgerald actually happened as far as the wide receiver, the phenom, the person we see today.

 "Had to wake him up, because my dad was pissed. My dad was like, 'What are you doing?'...my mom and my dad. You saw him take [the job] way more serious, and he was way more dedicated. I really think that shook him up enough to know that you don't have too many chances in life to keep screwing up."

 Fitzgerald wasn't a ball boy to just any receivers. The Vikings were led by a pair of future Hall of Fame receivers in Randy Moss and Cris Carter, who brought Minnesota to the brink of Super Bowl XXXIII after a 15-1 season. Over the next three seasons, Fitzgerald received a Ph.D.-level education in being a wide receiver and a professional football player. Without those relationships, without those hours of watching Carter and Moss, among others, Fitzgerald might never have been measured for a gold jacket.

 

 "No, I don't think so," Fitzgerald told ESPN when asked if he would be going into the Hall without those three years as a ball boy. "And I say that because I think me being around those guys and seeing players coming and going, guys blowing their money, getting hurt, just the underbelly of the league, I don't know if I would've been as focused on the big picture, stayed away from the distractions, not drink, not use drugs. All of the decisions you have to make as a young person that determine the trajectory.

 "I don't know if I would've had the insight or foresight to avoid those types of things."

 But he didn't avoid every temptation.

 

 CARTER REMEMBERS A TIME  when Fitzgerald took his "tricked-out Denali" to a car wash and it came back a little light.

 "Stole all the change out the ashtray," Carter said. "I said I hope he's good at football, because you're not going to be a good thief."

 Fitzgerald got close to Carter through Marcus, who used to babysit Carter's kids. Larry spent a couple of spring breaks at Carter's home in Florida to train. He still talks to Carter and his ex-wife Melanie Morgan -- "Aunt Mel" -- all the time.

 "They were just a really great family," Fitzgerald said. "And obviously he's a Hall of Fame talent, so to be able to pick his mind and learn from him was something that meant a great deal to me.

 "And to be able to have that type of knowledge with that proximity was not something that most people were able to have."

 The search for knowledge is what most impressed Carter.

 "Larry is a student of information," Carter said. "Everything he's into, he is deeply into it to an addictive level, and the lifestyle, the fanfare, playing the position, he could see as a youngster, 'Man, I know what I want to do.'"

 However, Carter, like a number of other Vikings, quickly noticed that Fitzgerald had the natural ability to merge his hard work and his thirst for knowledge.

 "We got hundreds of ball boys," Carter said. "Only one became a Hall of Famer because he's the only one that had the DNA."

 The impressions Carter and Moss made on Fitzgerald weren't limited to the football field.

 

 "And I'll never forget, one of the first camp practices, I always knew [Moss] played basketball," Fitzgerald said. "We were all shooting in the gym before practice started, and they had to walk through the gym to get to the locker rooms. And I remember him just grabbing the basketball and taking a few steps and just dunking it as he's walking through in flip-flops.

 "And I'm like, Jesus Christ, this dude is just so athletic. And so I think some of the freaky things that he would do every day at practice, they weren't things that you could really ... you could watch it in awe, but you know you never could do it."

 But there was one Moss trait Fitzgerald could emulate.

 "He's one of the few guys that I saw with that level of talent that had that work ethic," he said. "His work ethic was really good for a guy that was that talented."

 The admiration wasn't a one-way street.

 

 A GROUP OF about 10 Vikings that often included Moss, Carter, seventh-round pick Matthew Hatchette and quarterback Daunte Culpepper would attend Fitzgerald's high school games. They'd go to dinner after and made it a weekly thing during home-game weekends.

 Korey Stringer, who was a Vikings tackle at the time, once went to one of Fitzgerald's practices. When he saw Fitzgerald standing on the outside of a huddle at the end of practice, he yelled down from the stands for Fitzgerald to get in the middle of it.

 "It became that 'Hey, we got to help him out' type of attitude for us as a receiver group," Hatchette said.

 "He was one of the crew, basically," former Vikings running back Leroy Hoard said.

 

 It helped that Larry Sr. was a longtime Vikings beat reporter for the Minnesota Spokesman-Recorder, and was very close to Green. Fitzgerald Sr. died June 1 at the age of 71.

 "[Larry Jr.] was part of the family a little bit with his dad being the beat writer and Denny's main guy he talked to about the Vikings," former Vikings receiver Chris Walsh said.

 "He was our kid," Carter added.

 As Fitzgerald got more comfortable and as the receivers embraced him, he began asking questions. Lots of questions.

 "He was asking very specific questions like, 'OK, why'd you turn your hands over on the way you caught it like this, Cris, compared to turning your pinkies together?'" Hatchette recalled. "Stuff like that. 'How did you keep the defender on your backside when you were attacking the football?'

 "Little questions like that were way different questions that a kid would ask at that point."

 The receivers let Fitzgerald sit in on their position meetings, where he'd watch Carter reveal how  Detroit Lions  defenders would bang their fists together when they were about to check into a different play. It was in those meetings that he learned a valuable lesson from his time as a ball boy: how to read and recognize defenses.

 "I think you can be as good as you want, but if you don't know what the f--- is going on in the football field, you're not going to have very much success. You got to know what's going on," Fitzgerald said.

 "So, all of those things, I would recognize that just being able to sit in those meetings."

 After practice, after the receivers got their extra work in, Fitzgerald would catch passes from the Jugs machine, often with Hatchette. Walsh remembered Fitzgerald doing the same Jugs drills as the receivers, such as turning to catch the ball as it quickly approached or working the sideline. Fitzgerald would also run routes for quarterbacks who wanted to get in a few more reps. At one point, Carter told him to put on gloves and Fitzgerald was the only ball boy wearing gloves.

 "Well, I just thought you're going to get what you put in in terms of the work," Fitzgerald said. "And I saw those guys putting a lot of effort into getting better. And I knew that if I wanted to do that, then that was what was going to be required.

 "I was going to have to do the same thing, and I just learned the work ethic. I learned the detail. I learned the focus. And those are the things that really stood out to me."

 It was when Fitzgerald would catch balls that the Vikings started to realize his potential.
